Habitat_Description: This project includes habitat and hydrologic  restoration at the existing 77 acre Powell Creek Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 comprised of six plant communities including mesic and scrubby flatwoods, slough, hydric hammock, depression marsh, scrub with live oak and and floodplain with pop ash. These habitats are home to a variety of animal species including warblers, pileated woodpeckers, gray squirrels, rabbits and gopher tortoise, as well as feral hogs. The preserve is surrounded by urban development with extensive hydrologic alterations within and adjacent to it.
Restoration_Technique: Stormwater/Runoff Controls (only choose for natural habitat)
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Prescribed fire was conducted on 130 acres to restore habitat diversity, including some fire breaks and roller chopping.
Habitat_Description: This project includes habitat restoration in the Myakka State Forest comprised of a vast diversity of plant communities including pine palmetto flatwoods, oak hammock and freshwater wetlands with some invasive exotic vegetation.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Koreshan State Park Boomer Addition Restoration
Project_Description: This is a habitat and hydrologic restoration project that includes invasive exotic vegetation removal (Melaleuca and Brazilian pepper) restoration of altered hydrologic flows within and into the preserve.
Habitat_Description: This project includes habitat and hydrologic restoration at the existing 38 acre Koreshan State Park Boomer Addition Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 comprised of a mixture of native and disturbed habitats including oak hammock, pine flatwoods and some freshwater wetlands between urban development and the Estero River.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a habitat and hydrologic restoration project where invasive exotic vegetation of cogongrass and Melaleuca was removed, as well as restoring natural sheet flow.
Habitat_Description: This project includes habitat  restoration at the existing 339 acre Yellow Fever Creek Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 comprised of forested uplands, dry prairie, pine flatwoods and freshwater herbaceous wetlands with invasive exotic vegetation including cogongrass, Melaleuca and other exotic species throughout. The preserve includes the headwaters of Yellow Fever Creek, surrounded by urban development. Hydrologic alterations have changed the flows within and into the preserve. Plans exist to develop public facilities with hiking, picnicking and equestrian trails.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Dobbs Preserve Backes and Peterson Acquisitsions
Project_Description: This project is a new acquisition for protection and restoration and public access of mesic pine flatwoods, tidal wetlands and mangroves, adjacent to an existing preserve managed and restored by the non-profit Calusa Land Trust and it's volunteers.
Habitat_Description: This is a new acquisition of 2 parcels (Backes 2 acres and Peterson 6 acres) adjacent to the existing Dobbs Preserve managed by the Calusa Land Trust, comprised of mesic pine flatwoods, tidal wetlands, mangroves, saltmarsh and disturbed uplands with extensive exotic vegetation including Australian pines, Melaleuca and Brazilian pepper.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Exotic vegetation Brazilian pepper was removed by Lee County staff and volunteers.
Habitat_Description: This project includes habitat maintenance and restoration at the existing 126 acre Cayo Paleau Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 comprised of mangroves, tidal swamp, small amounts of coastal berm with Brazilian Pepper.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project that includes removal of Melaleuca and Brazilian pepper, preparing and conducting prescribed fires and planting long leaf pines on areas throughout the 730 acre preserve.
Habitat_Description: This project includes habitat restoration at the existing 730 acre Pine Island Flatwoods Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 comprised of nine plant communities including mesic pine flatwoods, freshwater marshes, tidal swamp, hydric hammock, coastal grassland, coastal berm, improved pastures and abandoned groves. The area has exotic vegetation including Melaleuca and Brazilian pepper and high fire fuel loads.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Six Mile Cypress Preserve North Addition
Project_Description: This land was acquired for habitat protection and habitat and hydrologic restoration. Future restoration on the parcel  includes correcting altered hydrologic flows within the preserve on the agricultural land and into the preserve from the surround urban lands. The native uplands and wetlands will be protected, and the agricultural lands will be restored, focusing on removal of invasive exotic vegetation.
Habitat_Description: This project acquisition of an additional parcel adjacent to the existing 750 acre Six Mile Cypress North Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 is comprised of pine flatwoods, oak hammocks, cypress sloughs, riverine wetlands and abandoned and historic headwaters of the Six Mile Cypress Slough. The native uplands, wetlands and agricultural lands include invasive exotic vegetation and have altered hydrology within and into the preserve.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Invasive exotic vegetation of Brazilian pepper was removed, followed by shoreline stabilization including sloping the bank, rip rap and native vegetation plantings. There are future plans for a canoe launch and nature trails.
Habitat_Description: This project includes habitat restoration and public access to the existing 9 acre Columbus G. McLeod Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. The property is comprised of an island in the Caloosahatchee River with five plant communities including mangrove and tidal swamp, mesic and hydric hammock with extensive Brazilian pepper and some shoreline erosion. The native habitats are home to a variety of animal species including white ibis, little blue heron, red shouldered hawk, West Indian manatee, American alligators and common moorhens.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Myrtle Slough Worch FARMS Rstoration Project
Project_Description: This is a riverine wetland habitat restoration project for restoring hydrology and water quality into Myrtle Slough and Shell Creek from an adjacent agriculture property by implementing agricultural best management practices through the Facilitating Agricultural Resource Management Systems (FARMS) program to reduce irrigation water needs and provide alternative water supplies and improved irrigation techniques for flatwood citrus operations. The project reduces reliance on mineralized groundwater (and mineralized subsequent runoff) by increased management of irrigation water using electrically operated surface water irrigation pumps and water filtration equipment.
Habitat_Description: This project involves riverine wetland habitat restoration project for Myrtle Creek and Shell Creek through hydrologic and water quality restoration at the adjacent 45 acre Worch tangerine grove in Charlotte County. The riverine wetland habitats have been adversely impacted due to changes in water quantity, timing and quality.
Restoration_Technique: Stormwater/Runoff Controls (only choose for natural habitat)
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a new land acquisition for preservation and restoration of habitat and cultural resources project. In the future, native vegetation will be restored by planting, invasive exotic vegetation removed, the historical home site restored, sections of hiking trail will be connected.
Habitat_Description: This is a new acquisition of the 28 acre Bailey Homestead Preserve on Sanibel Island by the Sanibel Captiva Conservation Foundation for habitat and cultural resource protection and restoration and public access. The parcel is comprised of native uplands and freshwater wetlands, plus some disturbed uplands, surrounded by residential development. The habitats support a variety of wildlife including bobcats, gopher tortoise, marsh rabbits, and song and wading birds.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is an acquisition project for habitat protection and restoration and public access to restore mesic pine flatwoods, tidal wetlands and mangroves and create nature based, low impact educational and recreational opportunities.
Habitat_Description: This project includes acquisition of the 80 acre Wildflower Golf Club by the Lemon Bay Conservancy to be restored to natural conditions and used as a nature park. The current habitats in the preserve include mangroves and tidal creek, plus extensive grass areas with invasive salt bush, Spanish needles, dog fennel and invasive exotic Brazilian pepper. Lemon Creek flows through the parcel, connecting a series of ponds, all of which are tidally influenced. Historically, the parcel had hydric pine/palmetto flatwoods and inland scrub in addition to coastal mangroves. The habitats currently support a variety of wildlife species including legless island glass lizards, soldier butterfly, little blue herons, common moorhens, eagles, black crown night heron, blue crabs, juvenile tarpon. The acquisition, restoration planning and completion are accomplished by the non-profit Lemon Bay Conservancy and volunteers.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Sarasota County restored native upland vegetation on this 8 acre previously disturbed grassy upland habitat by engaging local residents and elementary school with planning the uses of the  upland parcel surrounding a 3 acre stormwater pond. The local community helped design the park and participated in habitat restoration activities. The once unused open lot is a neighborhood park with a walking trail, gazebos, fishing pier, picnic tables, a fountain in the lake and offers environmental education and recreational opportunities.
Habitat_Description: This project is on 8 acres of previously disturbed grassy upland habitats on a county owned parcel with a 3 acre stormwater pond surrounded by an urban residential neighborhood that has been restored to native upland vegetation.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a habitat and hydrologic restoration project that includes preparing and conducting a prescribed fire, as well as removal of invasive exotic vegetation (Melaleuca).
Habitat_Description: This project includes habitat and hydrologic restoration at the existing 131 acre Pine Lake Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 comprised of cypress-pine communities, pine flatwoods, oak hammocks and riverine floodplain, with extensive invasive exotic vegetation (primarily Melaleuca), as well as hydrologic alterations, including a large borrow pit. The native habitats and borrow bit provide habitat for a number of wading birds including herons, egrets, sandpipers, killdeer and black-neck stilts, as well as American alligators. The preserve is located along the Imperial River floodplain. Lack of burning has reduced habitat diversity and increased fire fuel loads.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Oyster Creek Regional Park Invasive Exotic Vegetation Treatment
Project_Description: The project included removal of Brazilian pepper, Java plum and rosary pea by a volunteer crew.
Habitat_Description: The Park natural habitats include pine flatwoods, scrub and mangrove swamp along Oyster Creek, with areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Brazilian pepper, Java plum and rosary pea.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This habitat restoration project included prescribed fire (200 acres), roller chopping (40 acres) to reduce fuel load, and feral hog removal (10 hogs), to allow native habitats recover.
Habitat_Description: The Park native habitats include Tippecanoe Creek and oak scrub, scrubby flatwoods, pine flatwoods, coastal hammock, floodplain forest, salt marshes and mangrove swamps.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Amberjack Environmental Park Phase 2 Invasive Exotic Vegetation Treatment
Project_Description: Phase 2 included removal of Brazilian pepper and Lygodium by a volunteer crew.
Habitat_Description: The Park natural habitats include xeric oak scrub, scubby flatwoods and mangrove swamps adjacent to Amberjack Slough, with areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Brazilian pepper and Lygodium.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: The project included hydrologic restoration of previous agriculture drainage activities leading to Telegraph and Fetcher's Creeks, as well as removal of invasive exotic vegetation including cogongrass, guinea grass, Brazilian pepper, carrotwood and natal grass, allowing re-establishment of native vegetation.
Habitat_Description: The Preserve is comprised of several parcels managed holistically and native habitats include Telegraph Creek, wet and mesic pine flatwoods, wet and dry prairies, cypress and swamps, and freshwater marshes. The Preserve uses include active recreation, ranching, silviculture and farming.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Alva Scrub Preserve Phase 2 Habitat Restoration
Project_Description: The project included mechanical removal and herbiciding of invasive exotic species including cogongrass, guinea grass, Brazilian pepper, carrotwood and natal grass, allowing re-establishment of native vegetation.
Habitat_Description: The Preserve native habitats are comprised of mesic and scrubby flatwoods, oak hammock, wet prairie, floodplain swamp, and cypress head and swamps, with some areas of unimproved pasture.
Main_Funding_Source: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Gasparilla Sound/Charlotte Harbor Aquatic Preserve Phase 2 Scallop Restoration
Project_Description: Approximately 10 million bay scallop larvae, collected from nearshore waters in the Florida Big Bend area, were released over healthy seagrass beds just prior to the stage in their life cycle where they settle onto the seagrass and develop into juvenile scallops. An additional 18,000 juvenile bay scallops were raised to 5-20mm size and released, also in seagrass beds. Monitoring of adult populations and next year’s recruitment of larvae is planned. The project involved local, state and regional agencies, as well as volunteers.
Habitat_Description: The Aquatic Preserve native habitats include mangroves (red, white and black), seagrasses (turtle grass, shoal grass and manatee grass) and unvegetated submerged habitats which  support a great diversity of fish, shellfish, invertebrates and marine mammals including oyster, clams, shrimp, mangrove snapper, snook, dolphins and manatees. Seagrass and water quality conditions are adequate to support bay scallop populations, but sources of larvae are limited and red tide adversely impacts fledgling populations.
Lead_Implementer: Florida Sea Grant Extension Charlotte County
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: FY14 habitat restoration activities included roller chopping (200 acres) to reduce fire fuel loads and restore diversity, invasive exotic vegetation removal and treatment (5 acres) of Brazilian pepper, Melaleuca, Old World climbing fern, and cogongrass, and feral hog removal (125), to allow re-establishment of native vegetation.
Habitat_Description: The Parcel natural habitats include mesic flatwoods, hammocks, marshes, isolated wetlands and slough, with some areas of invasive exotic vegetation, including Brazilian pepper, Melaleuca, Old World climbing fern, and cogongrass, as well as feral hogs.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Major Park Yellow Fever Creek Preserve Phase 2 Invasive Exotic Vegetation Removal
Project_Description: Phase 2 included removal of Melaleuca, Australian pine and earleaf acacia by staff, contractors and volunteers, followed by herbicide treatment of new growth.
Habitat_Description: The preserve includes Yellow Fever Creek and a variety of upland and wetland habitats, including pine palmetto, oak hammock, forested uplands, dry prairie and freshwater herbaceous wetlands with extensive areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Melaleuca, Australian pine and ear-leaf acacia, surrounded by residential and urban development.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Port Charlotte Unit Phase 2 Habitat Restoration
Project_Description: Phase 2 included invasive exotic vegetation control (340 acres) of Brazilian pepper, cogongrass, carrotwood, Melaleuca, and natal grass, prescribed burning (27 acres) and feral hog removal (64).
Habitat_Description: The Unit native habitats include mesic pine flatwoods, scrubby flatwoods, salt flats, salt marshes, mangrove islands, embayments and several tidal creeks, including Tippecanoe, Sam Knight and Flopbuck. The pine flatwoods have high fire fuel loads and extensive areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Melaleuca, Australian pine, carrotwood and rosary pea, as well as feral hogs.
Main_Funding_Source: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Don Pedro State Invasive Exotic Vegetation Control
Project_Description: This invasive exotic vegetation control project included using herbicide to treat Brazilian pepper, cogongrass, carrotwood, Melaleuca, and natal grass, allowing re-establishment of native vegetation, including the imperiled coastal leather fern (Acrostichum aureum).
Habitat_Description: The Park native habitats are comprised of a variety of upland and coastal habitats, including mesic flatwoods, scrubby flatwoods, salt marsh, mangrove swamp, coastal strand and beach dune natural communities, with large amounts of Brazilian pepper, Australian pine, Melaleuca, and carrotwood, are adjacent to  the Gasparilla Sound estuary and surrounded by residential and urban development.
Main_Funding_Source: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Myakka River Deer Prairie Creek Preserve Habitat Restoration
Project_Description: FY14 habitat restoration focused on prescribed fire (344 acres) to restore diversity and allow re-establishment of native vegetation.
Habitat_Description: The Preserve native habitats include pine flatwoods, prairie hammock, seasonal wetlands and diverse wildflowers including St. John’s wort, tarflower and pine lily. The native uplands have heavy fire fuel loads and invasive exotic vegetation including Brazilian pepper, Australian pine, Melaleuca and cogongrass.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: South Venice Lemon Bay Preserve Habitat Restoration
Project_Description: FY14 habitat restoration focused on prescribed fire (17 acres) and roller chopping (15 acres) to restore diversity and allow re-establishment of native species.
Habitat_Description: The Preserve native estuarine, upland and wetland habitats include mangrove and tidal swamp, tidal marsh, coastal hammock mesic pine flatwoods and scrubby flatwoods, as well as submerged seagrasses in the adjacent estuary. There is heavy fire fuel load in the pine flatwoods and moderate levels of invasive exotic plants including Brazilian pepper, Australian pine and Melaleuca.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: FY14 habitat restoration focused on prescribed fire (2,460 acres) and feral hog removal (397), with some invasive exotic vegetation removal (10 acres) of cogongrass to restore diversity and allow re-establishment of native species.
Habitat_Description: The Reserve native habitats include pine flatwoods, upland mixed forests, lakes and seasonal wetlands which are home to gopher tortoises, bald eagles, roseate spoonbills and song and wading birds. The pine flatwoods have heavy fire fuel loads and there are areas of invasive exotic vegetation including cogongrass, Brazilian pepper, Melaleuca and Australian pine, as well as feral hogs.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: The acquisition is a Lee County Conservation 2020 purchase of 3.2 acres of native and disturbed pine flatwoods and mangrove habitat adjacent to Tarpon Bay and the Pine Island Sound estuary. The parcel will be managed jointly with the recently purchased adjacent parcel by the US Fish and Wildlife Service for preservation, restoration and resource-based recreational opportunities.
Habitat_Description: The Preserve is adjacent to the Tarpon Bay estuary and is comprised of a variety of coastal, upland  and wetland communities, including beach, mangrove, mesic pine flatwoods and hammocks, as well as a single family residence.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Ainger Creek Trails North Habitat Restoration
Project_Description: FY14 habitat restoration included invasive exotic vegetation  treatment and removal, mostly of cogongrass, and roller chopping to increase diversity and allow re-establishment of native vegetation.
Habitat_Description: The Parcel natural habitats include mesic flatwoods, hammocks, marshes and isolated wetlands, with some areas of invasive exotic vegetation, including Brazilian pepper, Melaleuca, Old World climbing fern, and cogongrass, as well as feral hogs.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: T Mabry Carlton Jr. Memorial Reserve Habitat Restoration
Project_Description: FY14 habitat restoration focused on prescribed fire (5,816 acres), Invasive exotic vegetation treatment and removal (1,800 acres) of cogongrass, Brazilian pepper, Melaleuca and Old World climbing fern, and roller chopping and timber thinning (885 acres), as well as feral hog removal (1,115) to restore diversity and allow re-establishment of native species.
Habitat_Description: The Preserve native habitats include a mosaic of uplands and wetlands including dry prairie, pine flatwoods, mesic hammocks, basin marshes and depressional wetlands. The pine flatwoods have heavy fire fuel loads and widely distributed invasive exotic vegetation, including Brazilian pepper, Melaleuca, cogongrass and Old World climbing fern, and abundant feral hogs.
Main_Funding_Source: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Sarasota County Lemon Bay Aquatic Preserve Scallop Restoration
Project_Description: Approximately 2,500 juvenile bay scallops, raised from larvae by Mote Marine Laboratory, were released over healthy seagrass beds during the stage in their life cycle where they settle onto the seagrass to grow to adulthood and reproductive stage. The project was conducted by county and research institution scientists and included monitoring of scallop survival.
Habitat_Description: The Aquatic Preserve native habitats include mangroves (red, white and black), seagrasses (turtle grass, shoal grass and manatee grass) and unvegetated submerged habitats which  support a great diversity of fish, shellfish, invertebrates and marine mammals including oyster, clams, shrimp, mangrove snapper, snook, dolphins and manatees. Seagrass and water quality conditions are adequate to support bay scallop populations, but sources of larvae are limited and red tide adversely impacts fledgling populations.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: San Carlos Park Mulloch Creek Habitat Restoration
Project_Description: The project began in 2006 with a demonstration yard planted at San Carlos Park Community Center. Starting in 2009 Melaleuca and Brazilian pepper were removed from the Drainage District canal bank lands behind two home, a trash pump was used to pull 'muck' from the canal and place it on the embankment, grass and air potatoes were pulled, and a diversity of native plants and trees were planted. In 2010, another 160 feet of shoreline was cleared of invasive vegetation and replanted with native shrubs and wildflowers. From 2011 through 2014 maintenance of exotic vegetation removal and native vegetation planting has been conducted regularly.
Habitat_Description: The project areas is located within a moderate density residential neighborhood built in the 1960s adjacent to a drainage district canal with steep banks, disturbed soils and mostly invasive  exotic vegetation including Melaleuca and Brazilian pepper, as well as large amounts of litter and trash.
Main_Funding_Source: Charlotte Harbor National Estuary Program, Southwest Florida Watershed Council
Lead_Implementer: Florida Gulf Coast University Department of Biological Sciences Nora Demers
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Myakka River State Park Phase 2 Habitat Restoration
Project_Description: Restoration actives included prescribed burning (8,620 acres), mechanical treatment of invasive exotic vegetation (82 acres), herbiciding of invasive exotic vegetation (1,244 acres)  and planting native species.
Habitat_Description: The Park native habitats include the Myakka River and many freshwater lakes, depression marshes, prairie, mesic flatwoods, as well as some areas of disturbed lands with invasive exotic vegetation including Phragmites, Brazilian pepper and Australian pine. Many areas have a high fire fuel load.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Highlands Hammock State Park Invasive Exotic Vegetation Control
Project_Description: This project included treating infestations of 2 Lygodium (fern) species in the hydric hammocks with herbicide.
Habitat_Description: The Park native habitats are comprised of a variety of upland and wetland habitats, including mesic flatwoods, scrubby flatwoods, wet flatwoods, scrub, hydric hammock, baygall and seepage slope natural communities, surrounded by private ranching, farm land and small residential housing developments. Large areas of the hydric hammock are heavily infested with Lygodium. Other species of invasive exotic vegetation include Brazilian pepper, Australian pine, Melaleuca, cogongrass and natal grass.
Main_Funding_Source: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Cape Haze Unit Phase 2 Habitat Restoration
Project_Description: Phase 2 included invasive exotic vegetation control (1,171 acres) of Brazilian pepper, cogongrass, carrotwood, Melaleuca, and natal grass, prescribed burning (92 acres) and feral hog removal which was necessary to reduce damage to native vegetation (220).
Habitat_Description: The Unit native habitats include pine flatwoods, oak scrub, tropical hammock midden/mound, freshwater and salt marshes, mangrove islands, as well as several tidal creeks, including Catfish, Widden, Sisters Pond, Trout and Big Muddy. The pine flatwoods have high fire fuel loads and there are extensive areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Melaleuca, cogongrass, guinea grass, Brazilian pepper and Old World climbing fern, as well as feral hogs.
Main_Funding_Source: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Cedar Point Park Phase 2 Invasive Exotic Vegetation Treatment
Project_Description: Phase 2 included removal of Brazilian pepper and rosary pea by a volunteer crew.
Habitat_Description: The Park natural habitats include pine flatwoods, scrub, scrubby flatwoods, mangrove swamps, salt marshes, and wetlands, as well as submerged seagrasses in the adjacent estuary, with areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Brazilian pepper, rosary pea and Lygodium.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: The acquisition is a non-profit Calusa Land Trust purchase of 2 acres of native and disturbed pine flatwoods and mangrove habitat adjacent to their existing St James Creek Preserve for preservation, restoration and public access to conservation lands.
Habitat_Description: The Preserve in adjacent to the Saint James Creek Preserve and includes some native slash pine and mangroves, but is heavily infested with invasive exotic vegetation, primarily Australian pine, which will be removed by Calusa Land Trust volunteers in the future.
Main_Funding_Source: Calusa Land Trust and Nature Preserve of Pine Island
Lead_Implementer: Calusa Land Trust and Nature Preserve of Pine Island
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: St James Creek Preserve Native Vegetation Planting
Project_Description: The project included planting 80 slash pines (5 gallon pots) by a volunteer crew, with  assistance from the local fire department providing water.
Habitat_Description: The Preserve is adjacent to the Matlacha Pass estuary and native habitats include mangroves, slash pines, cabbage palms and saw palmetto with small areas of exotic vegetation including Cesar weed, Lygodium and air potato.
Main_Funding_Source: Calusa Land Trust and Nature Preserve of Pine Island
Lead_Implementer: Calusa Land Trust and Nature Preserve of Pine Island
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: FY14 habitat restoration included roller chopping (42 acres) and feral hog removal (50) to restore diversity and allow re-establishment of native vegetation.
Habitat_Description: The Preserve native habitats are comprised of a mosaic of diverse natural communities including oak hammocks, pine flatwoods, scrubby flatwoods and seasonal marshes, including mature live oaks, epiphytes, Carolina jasmine and coral bean. There are small areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Brazilian pepper, Australian pine, Melaleuca and cogongrass.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Prescribed fire was conducted to reduce fuel loads and reduce encroaching hardwoods into wetlands and grassy uplands.
Habitat_Description: The Preserve native habitats include uplands, hammocks, swales and freshwater wetlands with a variety of plant species including gumbo limbo, mastic, Jamaica dogwood, Dahoon holly, pop ash, swamp bay, bald cypress, wax myrtle and mangroves which are home to numerous species of wildlife, birds and amphibians.

Project_Name: The Dunes Floating Vegetated Wetlands in Stormwater Ponds

Project_Name: Restoration of Native Ground Cover on Sanibel Island
Project_Description: As a result of invasive non-native invasions and development, native upland herbaceous plant communities on Sanibel are all but lost. During the past ten years, hundreds of acres of conservation and private lands on Sanibel Island have been cleared of invasive non-native vegetation as part of an effort to restore native plant communities. Restoration of upland herbaceous communities seems unlikely without specific additional efforts at reestablishment because the disturbance generated from large scale exotic removal results in the establishment of ruderal species, plants that are first to colonize disturbed land. Further, most of the desirable upland, herbaceous species are now absent or rare so natural recruitment is not likely. This project seeks to test methods of reestablishment of native ground cover following a restoration project. CHNEP is providing $4,000 toward this $9,633 project.
Habitat_Description: Upland and wetland grass and herbaceous cover.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

The large diversity of native plant communities can sustain a wide diversity of plant and animal species including many listed species. Very little of the natural landscape has been cleared and is mostly free of invasive, exotic pest plants. The wetlands filter impurities from surface waters. The land provides floodplain protection. The property has good access for public use, which may include hiking, bird watching, horseback riding, and nature study.
Habitat_Description: pine flatwoods, mesic (wet) pine flatwoods, wet prairie, cypress domes, and depressional marshes
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a Lee County COnservation 2020 acquisition. Alva Cypress Preserve (ACP) is a 675 acre preserve of five parcels acquired  from 1999 through 2008. The Preserve is located on the boundary between the Alva community and Lehigh Acres, with Joel Boulevard delineating the east boundary. The Preserve contains a diversity of plant communities including flatwoods, oak hammock, unimproved pasture and the 45 acre cypress head and pond for which the Preserve was named. This wetland area provides feeding and roosting areas for numerous listed wading bird species, as well as many other animals. At this time, the Preserve has an active cattle lease in the pasture area, so there is currently no designated trailhead or marked trails.
Habitat_Description: A diversity of plant communities including flatwoods, oak hammock, unimproved pasture and the 45 acre cypress head and pond
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: The project consists of a purchase of a variety of habitats including palmetto-oak scrub, pine flatwoods and seasonal wetlands. Views of scenic Hickey's Creek can be enjoyed from trail and overlook areas. The ecosystem presently supports the threatened Florida scrub jay and gopher tortoises. The Conservation 20/20 parcels within the Hickey's Creek Greenbriar Connector were purchased to provide connectivity for future hydrological restoration projects.
Habitat_Description: palmetto-oak scrub, pine flatwoods and seasonal wetlands
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: The state acquired 4,756 acres, which contribute to the area's water supply and are considered environmentally sensitive and which the water district had already purchased development rights for. The deal also included development rights to prevent houses from being built on another 7,630 acres.
Habitat_Description: Agricultrue lands formerly saw palmetto scrub, forested wetlands and hydric hammock
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Wild Turkey Strand Preserve is a 2,629 acre environmental preserve in the Estero Bay watershed purchased by Lee County Conservation 20/20 program in 2003 for its environmental qualities. The land is dominated by cypress, wet and mesic flatwoods, and freshwater marshes. This project will allow treatment of non-indigenous invasive plants from approximately 80 acres and restore emergency fire lines created by the Florida Division of Forestry during a 2007 fire. The plants include melaleuca (Melaleuca quinquenervia), Brazilian pepper (Schinus terebinthifolius), wetland nightshade (Solanum tampicense), Caesar’s weed (Urena lobata), West Indian marsh grass (Hymenachne amplexicaulis) and torpedo grass (Panicum repens). This restoration will prevent the invasive plants from spreading into the healthy, intact native plant communities. CHNEP is providing $20,000 toward this $41,617 project.
Habitat_Description: The land is dominated by cypress, wet and mesic flatwoods, and freshwater marshes.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Rocky Ford Protection Priority Site acquisition
Project_Description: This acquisition adds to the 1,391-acre site on the west side of the Myakka River has three miles of river frontage. Bald eagles, wood storks and various wading birds inhabit this area. Florida panther have been documented on this site
Habitat_Description: The site is mostly pine flatwoods, mesic hammocks and depression wetlands.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Converting Medians to Native Habitat - Sarasota County
Project_Description: Sarasota County is converting monoculture grass medians to native vegetation. The project occurred in phases and increased habitat and foraging for insects and birds. The project introduces residents to the appearance and care of native plants.
Habitat_Description: Highly impacted urbanized roadway medians
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Venetian Waterway Park (VWP) Exotic Removal from Segment 8
Project_Description: The Venetian Waterway Park is a 10-mile-long multi-purpose bicycle/pedestrian trail that includes the Shamrock Park and Nature Center, downtown Venice, picnic shelters, a canoe launch and access to Caspersen Park and Beach. The VWP connects to The Legacy Trail at the Historic Railroad Station and this exotic removal project begins just south of there. This project will allow eradication of exotic species along a section of the 10 miles of the greenway. Problem species include carrotwood (Cupaniopsis anacardioides), Brazilian pepper (Schinus terebinthifolius), lead tree (Leucaena), Australian pine (Casurina equisetifolia), Chinese tallow (Sapium sebiferum), rosary pea (Abrus precatorius), catclaw mimosa (Mimosa pigra), camphor tree (Cinnamomum camphora), air potato (Dioscorea bulbifera), Melaleuca (Melaleuca quinquenervia) and castor bean (Ricinus communis). CHNEP is providing $5,000 toward this $10,000 project.
Habitat_Description: Problem species include carrotwood (Cupaniopsis anacardioides), Brazilian pepper (Schinus terebinthifolius), lead tree (Leucaena), Australian pine (Casurina equisetifolia), Chinese tallow (Sapium sebiferum), rosary pea (Abrus precatorius), catclaw mimosa (Mimosa pigra), camphor tree (Cinnamomum camphora), air potato (Dioscorea bulbifera), Melaleuca (Melaleuca quinquenervia) and castor bean (Ricinus communis).
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Pine Island Flatwoods Preserve totals 719.4 acres and is made up of 6 separate acquisitions purchased in 2000, 2001, 2002, 2003, 2005 and 2008. The 2008 purchases encompassed an additional 34 acres. The Preserve is bordered by Stringfellow Road to the east, mangrove swamp and mudflats to the west, a future residential development to the north, and residential homes to the south. The northern portion of the Preserve has recently been connected the southern portion through the acquisition of an outparcel with an active palm nursery.
Habitat_Description: The Preserve consists of nine native plant communities, including mesic pine flatwoods, freshwater marshes, tidal swamp, hydric hammock, coastal grassland, coastal berm, improved pastures, abandoned groves, and unconsolidated substrate
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: The Preserve consists of twelve plant communities; one-third which are highly impacted from past uses. Historically, portions of the Preserve were used for agriculture and illegally as a site for outdoor recreation (camping, shooting/hunting and off-road activities). Ditches, berms, furrows, borrow and spoil areas, off-road vehicles (ORV), as well as invasive exotic plants have disturbed many portions of the wetland and upland plant communities at YPP. The dominant plant communities found on the Preserve are mixed mesic (flatwoods and hammock), mesic flatwoods and wet flatwoods. YPP contains a combination of wetland and upland communities that serve as important habitat for a variety of birds, mammals, reptiles and amphibians.
Habitat_Description: mix of pine flatwoods and xeric oak
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: 4,000 acres of exotics will be treated and 100 acres will be burned. Corkscrew Regional Ecosystem Watershed – is a 60,000-acre watershed spanning Lee and Collier Counties. CREW's majestic 5,000 acre marsh is the headwater for the entire watershed which includes the famous Audubon Corkscrew Swamp Sanctuary directly to the south.
Habitat_Description: pine flatwoods, marsh vistas, mysterious oak hammocks and pristine popash communities and invasive exotic melalucca
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Pine Island Preserve at Matlacha Park
Project_Description: Acquisition of 230 acres adjacent to the Matlacha Pass Aquatic Preserve for preservation and restoration of native habitat. The property, once restoration is completed, will provide stormwater storage and filtering, habitat for eagles, and wading birds and public access to natural areas
Habitat_Description: Mangrove swamp, scrub mangrove, pine flatwoods and improved pasture
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Shell Creek - Charlotte County Environmentally Sensitive Lands Program
Project_Description: Charlotte County purchased 380-acres straddling Shell Creek for preservation and water quality. Shell Creek flows into the Peace River. This acquisition will assist in improving water quality and hydrology in the Peace River
Habitat_Description: Freshwater creek with marsh and uplands
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Caloosahatchee Creeks Preserve is located north central Lee County in North Fort Myers on the northern shoreline of the Caloosahatchee river. The preserve consists of a total of 1290 acres. This acquisition was one acre.
Habitat_Description: Riverine shoreline, tidal influence, freshwater wetlands
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Six Mile Cypress Slough Preserve addition 360
Project_Description: The project adds an additional 2.5 acres to The Six Mile Cypress Slough (pronounced “slew”). The "Slough" is a 2,500 acre wetland in Fort Myers, Florida, that measures approximately 9 miles long and 1/3 mile wide. This linear ecosystem is home to a diverse population of plants and animals, including a few considered to be endangered. The Slough also serves as a corridor for wildlife by providing a safe route of travel. The Slough is a natural drainage-way, collecting runoff water from a 33-square-mile watershed area during periods of heavy or prolonged rainfall. During the wet season (June through October), a depth of 2 to 3 feet of water makes the Slough comparable to a wide, shallow stream. This fresh water flows southwest through the Slough and empties into the Estero Bay Aquatic Preserve.
Habitat_Description: mix of pine and cypress forest
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: The Myakkahatchee Creek (also known as Big Slough) drainage basin forms in Southeast Manatee County at the convergence of Bud Slough and Wild Cat Slough traversing Southwest through Sarasota County roughly 22 miles where it eventually flows into the Myakka River. This 38 acre acquisition project is one phase of a proposed multi-phase project.
Habitat_Description: Wetlands within the Myakkahatchee Creek corridor contain forested subtropical hardwoods. The land is habitat for gopher trotoises, osprey, red-shoudlered hawk and scrub jay
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Located within the City of Fort Myers, this property is located on the north bank of Billy's Creek canal directly west of Billy Bow Legs Park. The filter marsh is possible through a three-way partnership of government agencies. Lee County is buying the land; the South Florida Water Management District will help pay for the construction of the filter marsh with an $839,000 grant; and the City of Fort Myers will pay the remainder of the construction costs, do the construction work and maintain the filter marsh. The property's two native plant communities, cypress slough and oak hammock, will remain untouched by the filter marsh. The City will also provide hiking trails and a kayak launch. The site will eventually be listed on the Great Calusa Blue Way Trail.
Habitat_Description: Oak hammock, cypress slough and freshwater marsh abutting fresh to brackish creek
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Native Plant Demonstration Garden at Polk County Utilities Building
Project_Description: When Polk County residents pay their utility bills, they’ll be treated with a native plant demonstration garden. The demonstration garden will promote the nine principles of Florida-friendly landscaping and serve as a high-profile example to the residents of the county who will learn that using native plants, pervious surfaces, recycled products and appropriate drainage solutions can be beautiful and benefit the environment at the same time.
Habitat_Description: Native Florida grasses & wildflowers.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Recent restoration focussed on exotic invasive vegetation removal, primarily of Melalueuca, thinning pine trees to prevent pine beetle spreading and prescribed burning of 53 acres. Future stewardship efforts will restore palm tree nursery into a pine flawoods plant community.
Habitat_Description: Pine Island Flatwoods Preserve is a Lee County Conservation 2020 preserve with 730 acres located on Pine Island, including a recently acquired outparcel that connects 2 sections of the preserve that contained an active palm nursery. The Preserve consists of nine native plant communities, including mesic pine flatwoods, freshwater marshes, tidal swamp, hydric hammock, coastal grassland, coastal berm, improved pastures, abandoned groves, and unconsolidated substrate.
Main_Funding_Source: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This site in Punta Gorda is visited by residents and visitors alike. A butterfly garden approximately 20 x 50 feet in size will be created of native plant species. Signs will be installed and literature will be available to discuss butterfly gardening, emphasizing the need for host and nectar plants.
Habitat_Description: This site is a dredged and fill upland with disturbed upland habitats in a commercial marina use adjacent to Charlotte Harbor.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Ramblers Rest Campground Exotic Vegetation Removal
Project_Description: This project consists of the Myakka Wild and Scenic River Program treating Brazilian pepper on this site for 2 years using chainsaws and cut stump herbicide applications. The pepper is chipped onsite once it is cut with Rambler’s Rest equipment. Additional Brazilian pepper was removed from this site during the month of March 2009. The project is expected to continue into the future.
Habitat_Description: Disturbed forested wetlands and riverine floodplain with heavily infested with Brazilian pepper with some native live oaks and cabbage palms intermixed. The area where Brazilian pepper has been removed consists of native wetland species including saltbush and some leather fern.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Recent restoration activities at this site focused on removing fill and debris from the former sewage package plant that was bult in the wetlands, removed exotic invasive vegetation, especially Australian pines, restored freshwater fish refugia ponds, and replanted native wetland and upland plants where apprpriate.
Habitat_Description: The primary habitats at this site are rare barrier island freshwater wetlands and tropical hardwoodhammock.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: The purpose of the "Smokehouse Bay Preserve Restoration" project is to restore hydrology and native vegetation within the Smokehouse Bay Preserve, a Lee County Conservation 2020 parcel located in Lee County on northern Pine Island, adjacent to Matlacha Pass. This project will restore hydrology and native vegetation on 51 of those preserve’s 268 acres. The western portion of the preserve consists of an abandoned palm grove which slopes to mangrove swamp and Smokehouse Bay. Although much of the preserve consists of relatively intact native vegetation communities, the abandoned palm grove contains ditches and furrows. Non-indigenous invasive vegetation occurs both in the abandoned grove and within the adjacent mangrove swamp. The three phases of the project are: re-grading of the ditches and furrows to a more natural slope, treating non-indigenous invasive vegetation scattered throughout the abandoned palm grove, and planting of native plants (based on soil and historic aerials). A contractor will be hired to grade the site after an Environmental Resource Permit has been issued. Once graded, native plants will be purchased and installed by Lee County staff and volunteers from groups such as the Calusa Land Trust, Florida Gulf Coast University and from the Lee County Parks and Recreation volunteer pool. Category I and II exotic plant species on the Florida Exotic Pest Plant Council’s 2005 List of Invasive Species will be treated with an appropriate herbicide by cut stump, girdling, basal bark, or foliar treatments. It is most cost effective to treat these small scattered plants before they reach large sizes which have more ecological damage and are more costly to remove. Additional exotic plant treatments will continue over time, both on the abandoned palm grove and the mangrove swamp to the east.
Habitat_Description: Estuarine tidal mangrove adjacent to an abandoned palm plantation which was historically pine flatwoods, now inundated with invasive and non-invasive exotic vegetation and hydrologic modifications of ditches and furrows.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Recent acivities on this on-going project focused on exotic invasive plant removal, primarily Melaleuca, and roller chopping areas with high prescribed fire fuel loads.
Habitat_Description: Imperial Marsh Preserve is a Lee County Conservation 2020 preserve consisting of 5 parcels adjacent to the larger state-owned Imperial Marsh in southeast Lee County. The Preserve consists of a mosaic of both human-altered and natural plant communities including freshwater swamps, pine flatwoods, oak hammock, freshwater marsh and pasture lands. The majority of the sites are fairly new acquisitions.
Main_Funding_Source: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a new acquisition for preservation and restoration of riparian freshwater wetlands.
Habitat_Description: This is a new acquistion to create a new Lee County Conservation 2020 Preserve along Telegraph Creek near the Caloosahatchee River in Central Lee Countyl. The primary habitats include mesic pine flatwoods and freshwater wetlands adjacent to Telegraph Creek.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Four Mile Cove Ecological Park Restoration
Project_Description: Recent restoration activities at Four Mile Cove Ecological Park focused on exotic invasive vegetation removal, especially Brazilian pepper.
Habitat_Description: Four Mile Cove Ecological Preserve habitats include tidal mangrove swamps, tidal creek riparian vegetation, and disturbed uplands that have been dredged, ditched and filled.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Recent restoration activities at this park focused on removal of exotic, invasive vegetation, including Brazilian pepper (25 acres), cogan grass (7 acres) and Melaleuca (2 acres).
Habitat_Description: Major Park habitats include native and disturbed pine flatwoods and hardwood hammock.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Sanibel Dixie Beach Boulevard Mangrove Wetland Restoration
Project_Description: Recent restoration activities at this site focused on restoring tidal exchange to the mangroves east of Dixie Beach Boulevard by adding more culverts under the roadway.
Habitat_Description: The primary habitat found in this project area is tidal mangrove swamp, which supports a variety of bird and fishery species.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: The Carver Preserve was acquired for preservation and restoration in September 2008. This large mangrove area connects to State and Calusa Land Trust conservation lands to the north. With this acquisition, the entire Big Jim Creek inlet is now protected by conservation land. The Calusa Land Trust will assist the County with management of the preserve.
Habitat_Description: The Carver Preserve is a new Lee County Conservation 2020 Preserve with 189 acres located on Pine Island along Big Jim Creek, adjacent to state and private land trust preserve lands. The primary habitat is mangroves.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Recent restoration activiites focused on exotic invasive vegetation removal of Melaleuca, as well as roller chopping plametto to improve bird and wildlife habitat.
Habitat_Description: Alva Cypress Preserve is a 675 acre Lee County 2020 preserve located in northern Lee County, south of the Caloosahatchee River. The Preserve contains a diversity of plant communities including flatwoods, oak hammock, unimproved pasture and the 45 acre cypress head and pond forwhich the Preserve was named. This wetland area provides feeding and roosting areas for numerous listed wading bird species, as well as many other animals. There is also and active cattle lease in the pasture area.
Main_Funding_Source: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Recent restoration activities at Shell Creek Preserve focused on enhancing native habitats through prescribed fire.
Habitat_Description: Shell Creek Preserve is a Conservation Charlotte acquisition located in Punta Gorda. This site is the largest area of unprotected native habitat remaining along the unchannelized portion of Shell Creek. The character of the site is unusual for south Florida. From the waterline the creek banks rise almost vertically for several feet, up to 10 feet in some places, indicating that this creek is very old geologically in comparison to most south Florida waterways. Almost the entire site is made up of various upland habitat types, an unusual  feature for waterfront lands and a function of the highly incised creek. Landward of the xeric hammock are intermittent small areas of mesic hammock and scrub. Further landward are large areas of mostly high quality longleaf pine  dominated mesic flatwoods. Several small streams and one major creek enter Shell Creek within the site from both the north and the south. The site  contains three depressional marshes.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Recent restoration activities for the Sanibel River focused on removal of detritus, dead branches and exotic vegetation (primarily cattails) that restrictive natural flow of the river.
Habitat_Description: The Sanibel Restoration area vegetation includes native and disturbed freshwater wetlands and marshes adjacent to a small, shallow, low flow river on a barrier island, which support a veriety of wading bird and fishery species.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Recent restoration activities at Buck Creek Preserve focussed on enhancement of native pine flatwoods through mechanical thinning of trees.
Habitat_Description: Buck Creek Preserve is a Conservation Charlotte Preserve located in Cape Haze, Florida. The entire 80+ acre parcel is comprised of native habitats. The majority of the site is scrubby flatwoods and mesic pine flatwoods. These  flatwoods transition into coastal hammock and mangrove swamp along the creek. Buck Creek flows into Lemon Bay, an aquatic preserve and Outstanding Florida Water. The uplands on the site exhibit signs of fire suppression and many areas are succeeding into mesic oak and xeric hammocks. Mechanical restoration strategies will enable the property to be restored to its historical significance. These overgrown flatwoods are interspersed with open areas where  gopher tortoise burrows are present. There is also an active bald eagle’s nest on the site. Listed wading birds frequently forage along the banks of Buck Creek. It is one of the largest areas of unprotected native habitat remaining  on the Cape Haze Peninsula.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Recent restoration activities focused on removing hurricane impacted Australian pine debris with an excavator, burning debris piles, re-planting entire park in appropriate native species for each habitat with ~$450k in federal, state and local grants. This is a continuation of restoration activities that began in 2004 after Hurricane Charley and were completed in the spring of 2009. A variety of local, state and federal grants have supported the City of Sanibel's management efforts for this project.
Habitat_Description: Primary Bowman's Beach Park habitats include: dune, coastal scrub, tropical hardwood hammock and mangrove forest. The park is owned by Lee County and managed by the City of Sanibel.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Charlotte Harbor Preserve State Park Alligator Creek Restoration
Project_Description: Recent restoration activities on the Charlotte Harbor Preserve State Park Alligator Creek parcel focused on hydrologic restoration of 350 acres of saltmarsh, saltern and mangroves by backfilling over 35,000 linear feet of mosquito and drainage ditches.
Habitat_Description: The Charlotte Harbor Preserve State Park Alligator Creek parcel include native and disturbed mostly wetland habitats, primarily including tidal mangrove swamps, salt marsh and salterns.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Thorton Key Preserve was acquired by Conservation Charlotte in December 2008 for preservation, restoration and enhanced public access to natural resources.
Habitat_Description: Thorton Key Preserve is a Conservation Charlotte acquisition located near Englewood. Thornton Key Preserve contains 31+ acres in the middle portion of Thornton Key - an island in Lemon Bay just south of Stump Pass and east of Palm Island, within the Lemon Bay Watershed. The habitat value of the site itself is relatively good and contains moderate quality tropical coastal hammock that includes several rare plant species. The remaining habitats: mangrove swamps, salt barrens, and herbaceous marsh, are all of high quality. Brazilian pepper has infested the site to a significant degree, but has not yet displaced most of the native vegetation.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Recent restoration activities at this park include exotic invasive vegetation removal, of primarily Brazilian pepper and lead tree.
Habitat_Description: The habitats at this park consist primarily of tidal mangrove wetlands and salt marsh, as well as disturbed filled uplands and dredges borrow ditches with exotic invasive vegetation including Brazilian pepper and lead tree.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Recent restoration activities at this site focused on restoring riparian tidal creek wetlands by relocating an existing public water main, regrading the creek channel to it's original location, shapping the creek banks, creatting a littoral shelf and adding native wetland vegetation.
Habitat_Description: The primary habitat at this site is tidal creek riparian wetlands and mangroves.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Recent restoration activities focused on exotic invasive vegetation removal, primarily of Melaleuca. Future plans include prescribed burns within fire dependant plant communities
Habitat_Description: Yucca Pens Preserve is a 234 acres Lee County Conservation 2020 preserve, with 5 parcels, located in northwest Cape Coral adjacent to the Babcock-Cecil M. Webb Wildlife Management Area. The Preserve consists of twelve plant communities; one-third which are highly impacted from past uses. Historically, portions of the Preserve were used for agriculture and illegalas outdoor recreation (camping, shooting/hunting and off-road activities). Project_Name: Charlotte Harbor Harbor Preserve State Park Cape Haze Restoration
Project_Description: Recent restoration activities in the Cape Haze area of the Charlotte Harbor Preserve State Park focused on prescribed burning (79 acres plus 10 acres wild fire) and roller chopping (160 acres), with assistance from the Natural Resources Conservation Service Wildlife Habitat Incentives Program funding.
Habitat_Description: The Cape Haze area of the Charlotte Harbor Preserve State Park habitats include native and disturbed mesic pine  and scubby flatwoods and freshwater wetlands.
Main_Funding_Source: US Department of Agriculture National Resources Conservation Service Wildlife Habitat Incentives Program
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: The on-going Gasparilla Island Exotic Iguana removal program focuses on exotic invasive animal removal and removed over 4,000 Black Spiny-tailed Iguanas last year.
Habitat_Description: Gasparilla Island habitats include mostly disturbed upland barrier island scrubby vegetation with residential homesite landscapping.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Oscar Scherer State Park Scrub Jay Habitat Restoration
Project_Description: With the $10,000 in grant funds from TNC,Oscar Scherer State Park was able to outsource the roller chopping of 124 acres of scrubby flatwoods from June through October 2008. Consisting of 8 burn zones throughout the park. These zones were also treated for exotics treating approximately 5 acres of cogon grass. The roller chopping of these areas allowed us to have the zones ready for prescribed fire. Five zones were burned within 6 months of treatment. With the remaining 3 zones, our top priorities for burning when burn conditions are within prescription. The initial results from roller chopping the scrubby flatwoods before burning compared to other mechanical treatments used in the past are very positive and continued monitoring will be necessary. In the past when burning after mechanical treatment such as brown tree cutter and gyro cutter in the scrubby flatwoods mulch was produced in the process that would burn slow and not completely. Roller chopping produces no mulch and arranges the fuel in a good state (once cured) for burning. Some initial findings after burning these areas after roller chopping are; more fuels available to burn, more bare sandy spots, easier to light a backing fire on and a much cleaner burn.
Habitat_Description: Disturbed Scrub Jay habitat in Oscar Scherer State Park consisting of scrubby oak flatwoods infested with invasive exotic vegetation, including cogon grass.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Deep Creek Preserve was acquired by Conservation Charlotte in November 2008 for preservation, restoration and enhanced public access to natural resources.
Habitat_Description: The Deep Creek Preserve is a Conservation Charlotte acquisition located in Puntat Gorda. The site consists of numerous adjacent platted lots and two 20-acre parcels, located in the Deep Creek neighborhood, just east of the Peace River. The site is a mixture of scrubby flatwoods, mesic flatwoods, xeric and mesic hammocks, scattered depressional marshes and mangrove swamp. The western and northern portions of the site consist of mesic and scrubby flatwoods, with a few depressional marshes and hydric hammocks. The soils in this area support a vegetative structure that could provide suitable habitat for scrub-jays and other scrub dependent species. The southern and eastern portions of this site transition into high marsh and mangrove communities. Most of the upland areas were historically transitional habitat between mesic flatwoods and scrubby flatwoods. These uplands have characteristics of both these habitat types.

Project_Description: The Buckingham Trails Preserve was purchased for preservation and acquisition by Lee County Conservation 2020 in November 2008. Future activities include field work to develop Land Stewardship Plan and determine public recreational opportunities.

Project_Description: Shell Creek Preserve was acquired by Conservation Charlotte in April 2008 for preservation, restoration and enhanced public access to natural resources.
Habitat_Description: Shell Creek Preserve is a Conservation Charlotte acquisition located in Punta Gorda. This site is the largest area of unprotected native habitat remaining along the unchannelized portion of Shell Creek. The character of the site is unusual for south Florida. From the waterline the creek banks rise almost vertically for several feet, up to 10 feet in some places, indicating that this creek is very old geologically in comparison to most south Florida waterways. Almost the entire site is made up of various upland habitat types, an unusual feature for waterfront lands and a function of the highly incised creek. Landward of the xeric hammock are intermittent small areas of mesic hammock and scrub. Further landward are large areas of mostly high quality longleaf pine dominated mesic flatwoods. Several small streams and one major creek enter Shell Creek within the site from both the north and the south. The site contains three depressional marshes.

Project_Name: Peace River Restoration at Geraci’s property near Arcadia, Florida
Project_Description: 1000 feet of eroding shoreline with little-to-no riparian buffer was restored using Natural Channel Design, a Stream Bank Stabilization method. Heavy equipment was used to recontour the streambank and stabilize the sediments with trees, root wads, and coir-wrapped sod; this was followed by planting native vegetation to minimize erosion and mimic natural conditions. The Peace River Watershed contains 25 Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) and the reduction of sediment is critical to providing suitable habitat for these species, as well as recreational sportfish. Restoration was completed during February 2021. This project was a component of a multi-year effort implemented by FWC in partnership with the US Fish and Wildlife Service.
Habitat_Description:
Natural rivers and streams in which the stream flow, morphometry, and water chemistry have not been
substantially modified by human activities, or the native biota are dominant.

Project_Name: Conservation Foundation of the Gulf Coast Land Acquisition - Myakka Headwaters Preserve
Project_Description: A total of 363 acres near the headwaters of the Myakka River were permanently protected as part of a new preserve. The newly-named Myakka Headwaters Preserve protects the area where seven creeks converge into the Myakka River. The clear flowing water allows the creek bottoms to support submerged aquatic vegetation which are unable to grow in sunlight-blocked blackwaters found elsewhere on the Myakka.  The preserve contains floodplain forests that support endangered orchids and air plants. The preserve's marshland protects a Florida-endangered flower found exclusively in 12 counties throughout the state, lowland loosestrife. The preserve is also home to the gopher tortoise, a keystone species in Florida, as well as rare plants.
Habitat_Description: This particular area is full of many diverse habitats. The floodplain forests in the preserve contain trees such as Tupelo and Red Maple and support endangered orchids and air plants. The marshland forms a seasonally dry meadow with sandy ridges supporting lowland loosestrife, a Florida-endangered flower found in 12 counties and nowhere in the world. The preserve also contains more than a mile of uplands and oak hammocks. Also longleaf pine flatwoods are home to gopher tortoise. Oak hammocks.

This preserve also includes a significant area of scrub habitat, which previously was documented to have been used by federally-listed threatened Florida Scrub-Jays. The Caloosahatchee Creeks Preserve is home to a diverse abundance of wildlife, including the Gopher tortoise, West Indian Manatee, Wood Stork, tricolored heron, little blue heron, and least tern.  At the time of acquisition, approximately 500 acres of the preserve were identified as containing 75-100% coverage of invasive exotic vegetation. Wildlife management at the preserve will focus on providing optimal habitat for native 
species. Restoration of the disturbed areas, control of invasive exotic plants and application of prescribed fire will be critical restoration components to provide improved 
habitat for wildlife.

Project_Description: Exotics treatment of all FLEPPC-listed species were conducted throughout the entire 428-acre Hidden Cypress Preserve. Maintaining this land as open space has many benefits, including natural flood protection and preserving a wetland system that naturally purifies surface waters. These benefits have been further enhanced through restoration efforts including removing a large monoculture of melaleuca, an invasive exotic plant species.

Project_Description: In 2017, as part of a FWS take permit, the County was required to manage a previously established shorebird mitigation area located on Knight Island N. This last year, staff were able to obtain approval from FWC to treat the vegetation onsite using approved herbicides followed up with disking/tilling in an effort to stifle the vegetation growth long enough for nesting to occur onsite. In addition to the new management technique, a new predation study was implemented using Carolina Reaper pepper as a Coyote deterrent.

Project_Description: Exotics treatment of all FLEPPC-listed species was conducted throughout 53-acres of Pine Lake Preserve. native plants in selected critical areas in Myakka Headwaters Preserve. Located within a larger protected area, Myakka Headwater Preserve forms an important part of Flatford Swamp, the River’s largest forested wetland. The marshland forms a seasonally dry meadow with sandy ridges supporting lowland loosestrife, a Florida-endangered flower found in twelve counties and no place else in the world.

Project_Description: The project involved treatment of all currently listed FLEPPC Cat 1 and 2 exotic plants on 617 acres of the preserve, following the project area boundary to include exotics in the fenceline, along creekbanks, and firelines. A large population of gopher tortoises was present within the project area. All MUs have received at least one prior invasive exotic treatment sweep. Access to the project area was limited and a canal/cypress area had to be traversed to reach the eastern side. Water on-site may be hard to come by during dry season. Treatment for this project can be basal, cut stump, or foliar and the biomass can be left in place as long as it is not on or over a fence, gopher tortoise burrow, off property or on a fireline/trail.

In addition to the exotic treatment inside the preserve boundary, exotics were treated within all fire lines, trails, and fence lines including 12 inches outside of boundary fence lines. This project required 2 treatments on 40 acres. All FLEPPC Category I & II species were treated.

Project_Name: Caloosahatchee Creeks Preserve West Exotic Removal
Project_Description: This project was to treat the 288 acres in the project area for all FLEPPC listed Category I and II exotic plant species. The majority of the project area was last treated in 2021 with an exception of a small area around the bend in the railroad line. The project area included all areas up to the sod running along I-75. This treated all of the exotic grasses (such as guinea and mission) along the interstate just outside Lee County's fence. It also included all vegetation up to the dirt access road along the railroad. Within the project area, there was a three leaved vine, Causonis trifolia, located near the terminus of Pop Ash Creek Trail.
Habitat_Description: Shrub and Brushland, Mangrove Swamp, Upland Hardwood Forest
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This project involved a prescribed burn on approximately 107 acres of mesic flatwoods in North Port, Florida.
Habitat_Description: Mesic Flatwoods, Forested Woodland

Project_Description: Along floodplain wetlands of the Myakka River, Conservation Foundation of the Gulf Coast (CFGC) planted trees along the shoreline, planted herbaceous marsh vegetation within floodplain marshes, and treated an invasive exotic plant, called Old World Climbing Fern within floodplain forests.
Habitat_Description: 2123 Floodplain marsh, 2215 Floodplain swamp

Project_Description: Charlotte County acquired land as part of the Charlotte County Scrub jay Habitat Conservation Plan (HCP).

Project_Description: Lee County Conservation 20/20 acquired a 9.96-acre parcel within the Alva Scrub Preserve. This preserve consists of eight land parcels acquired between 1999 and 2019. The parcels extend from the southern boundary of Hickey Creek Mitigation Park, near Bateman Road, across to the eastern side of Edwards Drive. The preserve is home to many diverse plant communities, including mesic and scrubby flatwoods, oak hammock and cypress ponds. Gopher tortoises, great-horned owls and a variety of songbirds may be observed throughout the year. A Florida Panther has also occasionally been observed at the preserve. This 1,175-acre preserve also offers a 4-mile east-west corridor across which wildlife can travel.
Habitat_Description: Mesic and scrubby flatwoods, oak hammock and cypress ponds
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This project included the entire 66-acre area of site 107, and the entire 99-acre area of site 102. This was a retreatment sweep for exotic plant species throughout those preserve sites. The exotic density level was an average of 10% across the entire project area but varied in different areas. Exotic species viewed on this site included: brazillian pepper, melaleuca, cogon grass, earleaf acacia, downey rose myrtle, and old world climbing fern. However, all FLEPPC category 1 and 2 exotic species found within this preserve area were treated by the contractor. All exotics growing within these specified boundaries were included in this project.
Habitat_Description: Shrub and Brushland, Pine Flatwoods and Dry Prairie, Upland Mixed Woodland, Hydric Pine Flatwoods
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Lake Hancock is located in Polk County and is the headwaters of the Peace River. The lake has historically been regarded as hypereutrophic and as a result has been examined extensively for potential restoration options over the years. One project that has been highlighted in restoration management plans includes improving the aquatic vegetation in the lake. The Lake Hancock Revegetation Project will benefit the lake for many reasons including, providing fisheries and wildlife habitat, nutrient uptake, and reduction of sediment resuspension by lowering wind fetch. The project planted a total of 35 acres of the following species: Spatterdock, Pickerelweed, Alligator Flag, Jointed Spikerush, Southern Bulrush, and Eelgrass.
Habitat_Description:
(521) Lakes
Submerged aquatic vegetation
Main_Funding_Source: 50/50 cost share between Polk County and State of Florida
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Imperial River Boat Ramp Exotic Removal
Project_Description: This project included a single treatment sweep for all FLEPPC (newest list) Category 1 and 2 plant species found throughout the project area. These treatments included any target species found growing within the preserve boundaries. Highway 41 on the western side and small creek on the eastern side, along the boardwalk, and along the shoreline areas had never been treated. This was the initial treatment.
Habitat_Description: Mangrove Swamp, Hydric Pine Flatwoods, Parks and Zoos
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Hickory Swamp Preserve Exotic Control Project
Project_Description: Lee County Conservation 20/20 completed a exotic control project on 67 acres within Hickory Swamp Preserve. Located in Buckingham, Hickory Swamp Preserve is 66.5 acres surrounded largely by agricultural lands. The primary natural plant communities at this preserve are mesic and hydric hammocks and mesic flatwoods. By maintaining the upland ecosystems with prescribed fire and removal of invasive exotic flora and fauna, land managers have enhanced natural and managed wetlands on the preserve while improving wildlife habitat and water quality. The preserve will restore and protect the seasonal upstream headwaters of the Orange River, a tributary of the Caloosahatchee River.
Habitat_Description: Mesic and hydric hammocks and mesic flatwoods
Main_Funding_Source: Conservation Foundation of the Gulf Coast
