Project_Name: Hickey Creek Mitigation Park Exotic Control Project
Project_Description: Lee County Conservation 20/20 completed a exotic control project on 781 acres within Hickey Creek Mitigation Park. Hickey Creek Mitigation Park consists of a variety of habitats including palmetto-oak scrub, pine flatwoods, and seasonal wetlands. The ecosystem presently supports the threatened Florida Scrub-Jay and gopher tortoises. Environmental mitigation is an attempt to offset the detrimental impacts of development on a certain species or a type of native plant community. Exotic vegetation removal helps to restore the park to be a productive, functioning natural system. This exotic control project was completed in December 2022.
Habitat_Description: Palmetto-oak scrub, pine flatwoods, and seasonal wetlands
Main_Funding_Source: Lee County Department of Parks and Recreation
Lead_Implementer: Lee County Department of Parks and Recreation
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: The Florida Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) purchased a 11,958-acre conservation easement in DeSoto and Hardee counties within the Horse Creek Ranch Florida Forever project. This property provides a buffer for Horse Creek, a tributary of the Peace River, and will ensure the continued protection of the area’s drinking water supply. Protecting intact native wetlands in the Peace River watershed is crucial to the health of the Charlotte Harbor Estuary and the Gulf of Mexico. It's located within the Florida Wildlife Corridor and contains several threatened species, including the gopher tortoise, Eastern indigo snake, Eastern diamondback rattlesnake, and the Florida burrowing owl.
Habitat_Description: The site’s natural communities include mesic and wet flatwoods, bottomland forest, depression and basin marshes, mesic hammock, scrubby flatwoods, baygall, and blackwater streams. The natural uplands are mainly longleaf-pine-dominated mesic flatwoods with pockets of scrubby flatwoods on the highest elevations. More hydric wet flatwoods occur in the ecotone between the uplands and the Horse Creek floodplain. The remainder of the property is improved pastures and old agricultural fields.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Koreshan State Historic Site Invasive Vegetation Control

Project_Name: Wingate (Beker) Creek State Park Invasive Animal Control
Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 615 acre Wingate Creek State Park managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. There is an approved management plan for the park and management focuses on habitat protection and restoration, as well as public access and recreation. FY22-23 habitat restoration activities completed included removal of invasive animals (55 feral hogs).  Restoration is calculated at a 1:1 ratio hogs to acres.
Habitat_Description: Forested woodland upland habitat
Main_Funding_Source: Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) - Division of Recreation and Parks (DRP)

Project_Name: Four Mile Cove Preserve Exotic Removal
Project_Description: This project included a 52-acre area within the preserve. The entire preserve area is 194 acres. The exotic density level was an average of 10% across the entire project area but varied in different areas. Exotic species present on this site included: brazillian pepper, melaleuca, cogon grass, earleaf acacia, java plum, Australian pine, and old world climbing fern. However, all FLEPPC category 1 and 2 exotic species found within this project area were treated by the contractor. All category 1 and 2 exotic species growing within these specified boundaries were included in this project.
Habitat_Description: Pine Flatwoods and Dry Prairie, Hardwood Wetlands, Shrub and Brushland
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a habitat and hydrologic restoration project that focuses on filling ditches, removing berms & removing removal of exotic vegetation, including Melaleuca, Brazilian pepper, and earleaf acacia, as well as feral hog removal (over 120).
Habitat_Description: This project includes habitat and hydrologic restoration at the existing 268 acre Smokehouse Bay Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 comprised of freshwater marsh, salt flats and mangroves with  extensive invasive exotic vegetation (Melaleuca, Brazilian pepper, ear leaf acacia)as well as an abandoned palm tree grove with agricultural ditches and furrows as well as extensive mosquito control ditches. In addition, exotic feral hogs are common.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Powell Creek Preserve contains the northern most reaches of the natural channel of Powell Creek. To improve water quality in the creek and other downstream water bodies and to provide additional habitat for wildlife, an 18 acre filter marsh is being constructed on the preserve through a joint project with Lee County Division of Natural Resources. The project will divert water from both Powell Creek and the Powell Creek Canal into the filter marsh utilizing a pump. This water will flow through a series of created wetlands to allow sediment to settle out and excess nutrients to be absorbed by the wetland.
Habitat_Description: The Powell Creek Filter Marsh project (18 acres) is managed by Lee County and is located in the Powell Creek Preserve (77 acres) along Powell Creek, a tributary to the Caloosahatchee River in Lee County. The land uses surrounding the preserve include high density residential and disturbed pine flatwoods. The habitats in the preserve include mesic flatwoods, unimproved pasture, slough, scrubby flatwoods, hydric hammock, depression marsh and slough. The habitats support a diversity of native plants and wildlife, including pop ash, dwarf live oak, netted paw-paw, October flower, pileated woodpeckers, gray squirrels, marsh rabbits, and gopher tortoises, as well as feral hogs. The constructed filter marsh is designed to improved water quality entering Powell Creek and will be planted with native wetland species, including Dahoon holly, beauty berry, coco plum, cord grass, and pickerelweed.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 8 acre Pocono Trail Preserve managed by Sarasota County. Management focuses on habitat restoration and public access. Restoration activities focus on invasive exotic vegetation removal to improve wildlife habitat. FY12 restoration activities completed by county staff included 0.5 acres invasive exotic vegetation removal, including Brazilian pepper, Australian pine, and Melaleuca, as well as maintenance of trails. Hydrologic restoration of adjacent residential land uses is needed to further restore the habitats.
Habitat_Description: The Pocono Trail Preserve (8.2 acres) is managed by the Sarasota County Sensitive Lands Protection Program and is located on Shackett Creek in Nokomis, surrounded by high density residential land use. The native habitats include maritime hammock, tidal swamp and scrubby flatwoods. The habitats support a diversity of wildlife and birds, including gopher tortoises, grey squirrels, little blue heron, snowy egret, white ibis and wood stork. There is scattered invasive exotic vegetation, including Brazilian pepper, Australian pine and Melaleuca. Trails provide public access and wildlife viewing.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: T Mabry Calton Jr Memorial Reserve Restoration
Project_Description: This is an extensive habitat restoration project at the 24,565 acre T. Mabry Carlton Jr. Memorial Reserve Preserve managed by Sarasota County. Management focuses on habitat restoration and public access. Restoration activities focus on prescribed fire, non-native animal removal and invasive exotic vegetation removal to improve wildlife habitat. FY12 restoration activities completed by Sarasota County and Florida Department of Forestry staff included 3,800 acres of prescribed fire, 200 acres of roller chopping to reduce fire fuel loads, and 39 acres of invasive exotic vegetation removal, including Brazilian pepper, Australian pine, and Melaleuca, and removal of 1,291 feral hogs, as well as road and trail maintenance. Cost estimates are for Sarasota County contributions to prescribed fire only.
Habitat_Description: T. Mabry Carlton Jr. Memorial Reserve (24,565 acres) is managed by the Sarasota County Environmentally Sensitive Lands Protection Program. The preserve is located along the Myakka River, a designated Wild and Scenic River, east of Nokomis. The preserve was purchased for natural resource protection, nature based recreation and for a well field for public drinking water. The mosaic of native and upland and wetland habitats includes dry prairie, pine flatwoods, mesic hammocks and seasonal wetlands. The habitats support a great diversity of wildlife, birds and native plants including white-tailed deer, wild turkey, bobcats, swallow-tailed kites, wading birds, pine lily, tarflower and purple iris. The pine flatwoods have heavy fire fuel loads, there is widely distributed invasive exotic vegetation, including Brazilian pepper, Australian pine, Melaleuca, cogongrass and an abundance of feral hogs. Extensive motor vehicle and foot trails provide public access and wildlife viewing.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a habitat and hydrologic restoration project at the 2,654 acre Prairie Pines Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. A management plan has been developed for the Preserve which focuses on habitat and hydrologic restoration, as well as public access, including hiking and horseback riding. Activities include restoration of hydrology from off-road vehicle trails and removal of invasive exotic plants and exotic animals. FY12 restoration activities completed by Lee County staff and volunteers included removal of 150 feral hogs and Melaleuca and treatment of Guinea grass, old world climbing fern and cogongrass, as well as trail and sign maintenance.
Habitat_Description: The Prairie Pines Preserve is managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 and is comprised of a mosaic of several native plant communities, including wet and mesic flatwoods, depression marshes, wet prairies, prairie hammocks, a small baygall, and a small area of abandoned pasture. Some areas are disturbed by illegal off-road vehicles and past agricultural practices. There are extensive invasive exotic plants including cogongrass, Melaleuca and Brazilian pepper, as well as feral hogs.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: San Carlos Bay-Bunche Beach Preserve Restoration
Project_Description: This project includes habitat restoration at the existing 704 acre San Carlos Bay Bunche Beach Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. A management plan has been developed for the Preserve which focuses on restoration of upland, wetland and beach habitats, as well as public access, education and stewardship. Environmental educational activities are provided to the Lee County Public Schools, Edison College, FL Gulf Coast University and the public. FY12 Restoration activities completed by staff, volunteers and FL Gulf Coast University students include removal of over 500 pounds of invasive exotic vegetation and trash, as well as volunteer guided nature walks.
Habitat_Description: Preserve contains wetland areas such as tidal swamp, an extensive tidal creek system, coastal grasslands, coastal berms that define the southern border and extremely productive seagrass beds and mudflats that provide habitat and food for both fish and a wide variety of birds. The Preserve includes the shoreline of Rock Creek and beach along San Carlos Bay.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This project includes habitat restoration at the 67 acre Flag Pond Reserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. The site includes five wetland habitats and a fallow farm field, surrounded by residential development and a business park. A management plan for the preserve is being developed which will guide habitat and hydrologic restoration. No plans are included for public amenities at this site because the hydric soils and wetland plan communities are under water much of the year. During FY12, staff and volunteers completed initial treatment of invasive exotic plant species including Brazilian pepper, Australian pine and Melaleuca.
Habitat_Description: Flag Pond Preserve is managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 and is comprised of six plant communities including basin swamp, fallow farm land, mesic and wet flatwoods, mesic hammock, and wet prairie. The Preserve provides habitat for a variety of animal species, including white ibis, great egret, Florida cottonmouth and Florida apple snail.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This project includes acquisition of 5 acres of native and disturbed upland an wetland habitats adjacent to the existing Caloosahatchee Creeks Preserve (now totaling 1295 acres) managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 for habitat protection and restoration and public access and education. In the future, native vegetation will be restored by plantings, invasive exotic vegetation will be removed and natural hydrology will be restored as much as possible. A management plan is being developed for the parcel by Lee County Conservation 2020 which will include public access and education about the native habitats and restoration activities.
Habitat_Description: This is a new acquisition of 5 acres adjacent to the existing Caloosahatchee Creeks Preserve (now totaling 1295 acres) managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. The habitats are comprised of oak hammocks, pine flatwoods and mangroves, as well as extensive areas of exotic vegetation including Melaleuca, Brazilian peppercogongrass, Guinea grass, Lygodium, Wedelia, and air potato.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Charlotte Harbor Preserve State Park Cape Coral Restoration
Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 7,951 acre Cape Coral Management Area of the Charlotte Harbor Preserve State Park managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. There is an approved management plan for the area and management focuses on habitat restoration and public access. Restoration activities focus on prescribed fire and removal of non-native vegetation and animals, to improve wildlife habitat. FY12 restoration activities completed included 143 acres of prescribed fire, as well as road and trail maintenance.
Habitat_Description: The Cape Coral Management Area (7,951 acres) of the Charlotte Harbor Preserve State Park is managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. The Cape Coral Management Area is located along the east shore of Charlotte Harbor in Charlotte in Charlotte County and Matlacha Pass in Lee County. The habitats include primarily saltwater wetlands and marshes, mangroves, small stands of slash pines and tidal creeks. The tidal creeks include Yucca Pen, Allen, Annie’s, Big Dead, Gator Slough, Underhill, Oyster and Jewfish, which drain to the estuaries and seagrasses of the Gasparilla Sound/Charlotte Harbor and Matlacha Pass Aquatic Preserves. The habitats support a great diversity of wildlife, birds, fish and native plants including bob cat, osprey, great blue heron, snook, sea trout and manatee. There are extensive areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Brazilian pepper, Australian pine, Melaleuca, cogongrass, and old world climbing fern.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Ann Dever Memorial Oyster Creek Regional Park Restoration
Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 120 acre Ann Dever Memorial Oyster Creek Regional Park managed by the Charlotte Harbor Environmental Center and Charlotte County. Management of the park focuses on habitat restoration and public access, including hiking trails and boardwalks. Restoration activities focus on removal of invasive exotic plants to improve wildlife habitat. FY12 restoration activities completed by staff and volunteers included treatment of Brazilian pepper, Java plum and Melaleuca. In addition, existing trails and boardwalks were maintained for public access to the park.
Habitat_Description: Ann Dever Memorial Oyster Creek Regional Park (120 acres) is managed by the Charlotte Harbor Environmental Center and Charlotte County near Englewood. The habitats are comprised of old growth pines, scrub and mangrove fridge along Oyster Creek. The habitats support a great diversity of wildlife, birds, invertebrates and fish, including bob cat, bald eagle, oyster catchers and mangrove snapper. There are some areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Brazilian pepper, Java plum and Melaleuca. An observation platform and the boardwalk crossing Oyster Creek displays the variety of birds that utilize Oyster Creek and the surrounding mangroves.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: South Venice Lemon Bay Preserve Restoration
Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 22 acre South Venice Lemon Bay Preserve managed by Sarasota County. Management focuses on habitat restoration and public access. Restoration activities focus on prescribed fire and invasive exotic vegetation removal to improve wildlife habitat. FY12 restoration activities completed by Sarasota County and Florida Department of Forestry staff included 14 acres of prescribed fire, 5 acres of roller chopping to reduce fire fuel loads and 5 acres of invasive exotic vegetation removal, including Brazilian pepper, Australian pine, and Melaleuca, as well as maintenance of trails. Cost estimates for Sarasota County contributions to prescribed fire only.
Habitat_Description: South Venice Lemon Bay Preserve (222 acres) is managed by the Sarasota County Environmentally Sensitive Lands Protection Program and is located between the Venice Inlet and high density residential land uses. The habitats in the preserve are comprised a variety of upland and wetland coastal habitats, including tidal swamp, tidal marsh, coastal hammock and upland communities such as mesic and scrubby flatwoods, and a restored wetland slough. These habitats supports a variety of native plant and species such as mangroves, cord grasses, oak species, lupine, palafox, coontie, Curtis’s milkweed, gopher tortoises, Florida scrub-jays, bald eagles, otters, eastern coachwhip. A variety of plants are also represented, specifically, visitors may see Boardwalks afford visitors access across the recreated and restored wetland slough. There are high fire fuel loads in the scrubby and pine flatwoods, and invasive exotic vegetation throughout the preserve, including Australian pine, Brazilian pepper & Melaleula.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 80 acre Buck Creek Preserve managed by the Charlotte Harbor Environmental Center and Charlotte County. Management of the preserve focuses on habitat restoration and public access, including hiking trails. Restoration activities focus on removal of invasive exotic plants to improve wildlife habitat. FY12 restoration activities completed by staff and volunteers included treatment of Brazilian pepper, Java plum and Melaleuca to improve habitat for wildlife. In addition, existing trails were maintained for public access to the preserve.
Habitat_Description: Buck Creek Preserve (80+ acres) is managed by the Charlotte Harbor Environmental Center and Charlotte County near Englewood, along Buck Creek, a tributary to Lemon Bay Aquatic Preserve. The habitats are comprised of scrubby flatwoods and mesic pine flatwoods transitioning into coastal hammock and mangrove swamp. There are two freshwater marshes in the preserve. The habitats support a great diversity of wildlife, birds and fish, including gopher tortoises which are commonly seen, bald eagles and several species of wading birds, especially in the mangrove fringe along the creek. There are some areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Brazilian pepper, Java plum and Melaleuca. Trails allow public access and wildlife viewing in the park.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project on the 614 acre Jelks Preserve managed by Sarasota County. Management focuses on habitat restoration and public access. The preserve is one of the publicly-owned properties bordering the Wild and Scenic Myakka River, forever protecting a piece of the riverine floodplain. Restoration activities focus on removal of invasive exotic vegetation to improve wildlife habitat. FY12 restoration activities completed by staff and volunteers included 2 acres of Brazilian pepper, Australian pine, Melaleuca and cogon grass treatment and removal.
Habitat_Description: The Jelks Preserve (614 acres) is managed by the Sarasota County Environmentally Sensitive Lands Protection Program and was purchased through a generous contribution from the Jelks Family Foundation. The preserve is located along the Myakka River, a designated Wild and Scenic River, west of Venice. The habitats are comprised of a mosaic of diverse natural communities including oak hammocks, pine flatwoods, scrubby flatwoods and seasonal marshes. The habitats support a great variety of wildlife, birds, fish and native wildflowers, including mature live oaks, epiphytes, gopher tortoises, swallowtail butterflies, swallow-tailed kites, song birds, Carolina jessamine and coral bean. Trails provide public access and wildlife viewing and there are three access points to the river. There are small areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Brazilian pepper, Australian pine, Melaleuca and cogongrass.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 145 acre Manasota Scrub Preserve managed by Sarasota County. Management focuses on habitat restoration and public access. Restoration activities focus on prescribed fire and invasive exotic vegetation removal to improve wildlife habitat. FY12 restoration activities completed by Sarasota County and Florida Department of Forestry staff and volunteers included roller chopping of 15 acres in preparation of prescribed fire and removal of 3 acres of Brazilian pepper, Australian pine and Melaleuca.
Habitat_Description: The Manasota Scrub Preserve (145 acres) is managed by the Sarasota County Environmentally Sensitive Lands Protection Program. The preserve is located near the headwaters of Forked Creek, a tributary to Lemon Bay Aquatic Preserve near Englewood, surrounded by moderate density residential land uses. The native habitats both upland and wetland habitats, including pine flatwoods, depressional marsh, maple swamp and scrub. The habitats support a diversity of wildlife and native vegetation, including gopher tortoises, northern quail, swallowtail butterflies, great horned owls. grassleaf goldenaster and blazing star. The pine flatwoods have heavy fuel fire loads and areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Brazilian pepper, Australian pine and Melaleuca. Trails and a 330 foot boardwalk provide public access and wildlife viewing.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: The Briarcliff Filter Marsh Project is managed by Lee County and is implemented to improve water quality. The project is located along Briarcliff Canal which leads to Ten Mile Canal before entering Mullock Creek, a tributary to Estero Bay Aquatic Preserve. The project consists of a constructed 15 acre filter marsh designed to provide wetlands that will filter water from the surrounding residential and industrial land uses and impervious areas. Water will enter the filter marsh by two control structures and a steel sheet-pile weir was installed to aid in the dry season water conservation.
Habitat_Description: The Briarcliff Filter Marsh project (15 acres) is managed by Lee County and is located adjacent to Briarcliff Canal, near Ten Mile Canal in southeast Lee County. The surrounding land uses include low density residential and disturbed pine flatwoods. The constructed filter marsh is designed to filter water leaving the Briarcliff Canal as it enters Ten Mile Canal. The water levels in the marsh are controlled by 2 structures and a weir in order to provide appropriate water levels year around to support the planted freshwater wetland, emergent and submerged vegetation, including cypress, salt bush, waxy myrtle, cord grass, beak rush, pickerelweed, sedge, giant bulrush and spatterdock.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is an extensive habitat restoration project at the 37,199  acre Myakka River State Park managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. There is an approved management plan for the park and management focuses on habitat and hydrologic restoration and public access. Restoration activities focus on prescribed fire and removal of non-native vegetation and animals, to improve wildlife habitat. FY12 restoration activities completed included 10,688 acres of prescribed fire, as well as exotic plant and animal removal and trail maintenance.
Habitat_Description: Myakka River State Park (37,199 acres) is managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection and is located along the Myakka River, a designated Wild and Scenic River, in Manatee and Sarasota Counties. A mosaic of 11 upland and wetland habitats occur in the park, including dry prairie, mesic flatwoods, prairie hammocks, scrubby flatwoods, basin swam, baygall, depression marsh, cypress dome, floodplain marsh, blackwater stream and 2 riverine floodplain lakes. The habitats support a great diversity of wildlife, birds, fish and native plants including bob cat, snapping and mud turtles, wood stork, sandhill crane, roseate spoonbill, cypress, oak and wildflowers. The pine flatwoods have heavy fire fuel loads and there are high numbers of feral hogs, and extensive areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Brazilian pepper, Melaleuca, cogongrass, world climbing fern, air potato, and hydrilla.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This project includes habitat restoration at the 4.3 acre Mullock Creek Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. A management plan for the Preserve has been developed which focuses on habitat and hydrologic restoration on the native and disturbed wetlands and uplands. However, public access is not planned due to the small size and location, limiting access points. FY12 restoration activities include treating of invasive exotic vegetation, including Melaleuca, Brazilian pepper, Java plum, earleaf acacia.
Habitat_Description: Mullock Creek Preserve is managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 and is comprised of seven plant communities including wetland forested mixed, temperate hardwood, xeric oak, pine-mesic oak, exotic wetland hardwood, disturbed lands, and a portion of the a tributary to Mullock Creek. The drier xeric oak community is home to a small population of state-listed Gopher tortoises and the flowing creek supports American alligators.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This project includes habitat and hydrologic restoration at the 268 acre Smokehouse Bay Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. A management plan has been developed for the Preserve which focuses on habitat and hydrologic restoration, including invasive exotic vegetation and animal removal and back filling ditches. FY12 restoration activities completed by staff and contractors included restoring the natural elevation on the abandoned agriculture fields, backfilling the old mosquito control ditches, removing Brazilian pepper and Australian pines, and removing 90 feral hogs.
Habitat_Description: Smokehouse Bay Preserve is managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 and is comprised of freshwater marsh, salt flats and mangroves with extensive invasive exotic vegetation, including Melaleuca, Brazilian pepper, ear leaf acacia, as well as an abandoned palm tree grove with agricultural ditches and furrows as well as extensive mosquito control ditches. In addition, exotic feral hogs are common.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Major Park Yellow Fever Creek Preserve Restoration
Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 195 acre Major Park Yellow Fever Creek Preserve managed by the City of Cape Coral for ecosystem restoration and public access and environmental education. Management activities on the parcel are coordinated between the City of Cape Coral and the Lee County Conservation 2020 program and focus on invasive exotic plant removal and hydrologic restoration, as well as public facilities for hiking. FY12 restoration activities completed by contractors, staff and volunteers included removal of Melaleuca, Australian pine and earleaf acacia. The work was done at no cost to the City of Cape Coral because the contractor received the wood as payment for their work. Herbicide treatment of new growth will begin in the fall of 2012 and the herbicides were provided by the Florida State Herbicide Bank. All survey work was done by the City of Cape Coral’s Environmental Resources Division.
Habitat_Description: Major Park Yellow Fever Creek Preserve is managed the City of Cape Coral and is comprised of a variety of upland and wetland habitats, including pine palmetto, oak hammock, forested uplands, dry prairie and freshwater herbaceous wetlands with extensive areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Melaleuca, Australian pine and earleaf acacia. The preserve includes parts of Yellow Fever Creek, is adjacent to a Lee County Conservation 2020 preserve and is surrounded by residential and urban development.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Oyster Creek Exotic Plant Removal and Flow Enhancement
Project_Description: The Oyster Creek Exotic Vegetation and Flow Enhancement project is a habitat and hydrologic restoration project conducted by the Charlotte County Stormwater Engineering Department and consisted of removing invasive exotic vegetation, primarily Brazilian pepper on 17 acres land adjacent to Oyster Creek to improve habitat diversity and restore more natural runoff patterns. The restoration was conducted by hand with manually operated equipment, without the use of heavy vehicles to avoid adverse impacts to native vegetation and alterations to runoff patterns.
Habitat_Description: The Oyster Creek Exotic Vegetation Removal project is located in Englewood and managed by Charlotte County Stormwater, and is primarilly comprised of riparian wetlands, with some remaining pine-palmetto flatwoods and oak hammock, with invasive exotic vegetation, primarily Brazilian pepper, and areas of mowed grassy fields. The area is surrounded by residential land use with highly altered hydrology.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 69 acre Oasis Woods Park managed by the City of Cape Coral for ecosystem restoration and public access and environmental education. The park includes to parcels and management activities on the parcel are focus on invasive exotic plant removal and hydrologic restoration, as well as public facilities for hiking. FY12 restoration activities completed by contractors, staff and volunteers included removal of Melaleuca, Australian pine and earleaf acacia. The work was done at no cost to the City of Cape Coral because the contractor received the wood as payment for their work. Herbicide treatment of new growth will begin in the fall of 2012 and the herbicides were provided by the Florida State Herbicide Bank. All survey work was done by the City of Cape Coral’s Environmental Resources Division.
Habitat_Description: Oasis Woods Park is managed the City of Cape Coral and is comprised of a variety of upland and wetland habitats, including forested uplands, pine palmetto, oak hammock and dry prairie with extensive areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Melaleuca, Australian pine and earleaf acacia. The Park includes 2 parcels and is surrounded by residential and urban development.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This project is the acquisition of 17 acres of forested wetlands and cypress adjacent to the existing Corkscrew Regional Ecosystem Watershed Preserve (now totaling 30.5 acres) managed by Lee County 2020 for preservation and restoration of cypress and other forested wetlands adjacent to existing preserves. In the future, exotic vegetation will be removed and natural hydrology will be restored to the extent possible. A management plan is being developed for the preserve by Lee County Conservation 2020 which will include public access and education about the native habitats and restoration activities.
Habitat_Description: The Corkscrew Regional Ecosystem Watershed Preserve is a Lee County Conservation 2020 acquisition located in Lee County adjacent to the Pine Lake Conservation Preserve and the Corkscrew Regional Ecosystem Watershed. The primary habitats includes forested wetlands and cypress, which provide aquifer recharge, natural flood protection and water purification, and support such wildlife as the Florida panther and black bear.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This project includes habitat restoration at the 434 acre Hickey’s Creek Greenbriar Connector Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. A management plan is being developed for the Preserve, but the preserve does not currently have hiking trails or parking. Restoration activities focus on invasive exotic vegetation removal and prescribed fire. In FY 12, a prescribed fire on 28 acres on the pasture portion (Parcel 4) of the preserve was completed and the remaining Brazilian pepper on the Parcel was destroyed.
Habitat_Description: Hickey’s Creek Greenbriar Connector is a Lee County Conservation 2020 preserve comprised of   pine flatwoods, scrubby flatwoods, freshwater marshes, cypress swamps, hardwood hammocks and oak-palm forests
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This project includes habitat restoration at the existing 60 acre Orange River Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. A management plan has been completed for the preserve which focuses on invasive exotic plant removal, prescribed fire and native vegetation planting, as well as potential public access, including a boardwalk for manatee viewing. FY12 restoration activities completed by staff and volunteers included roller chopping overgrown areas of saw palmetto, removal of Melaleuca and Brazilian pepper and planting of native slash pines.
Habitat_Description: Orange River Preserve is managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 and is comprised of 3 distinct plant communities along the Orange River, including:  scrubby flatwoods, mesic hammock, and tidal swamp, including 3 species of mangrove, pond apple and leather fern, as well as invasive exotic vegetation including Melaleuca and Brazilian pepper.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 59 acre Matanzas Pass Preserve managed by Lee County 2020. A management plan has been developed for the Preserve which focuses on invasive exotic plant removal, native vegetation planting, debris removal and public educational and recreational activities, including boardwalks, trails and canoe/kayak launch. A native plant and animal species list has been developed for the preserve. FY12 restoration activities conducted by staff and volunteers included removal of air potato, Brazilian pepper and Australian pine, planting native wildflowers and trail maintenance.
Habitat_Description: Mantanzas Pass Preserve is a Lee County Conservation 2020 Preserve comprised primarily of tidal swamp and is dominated by mangrove forests, coastal grasslands, and oak hammocks, along with the only maritime oak community remaining on Fort Myers Beach. The Preserve boarders the Estero Bay Aquatic Preserve.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Six Mile Cypress Slough Preserve Restoration
Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project in the 2,267 acre Six Mile Cypress Slough Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. A management plan has been prepared for the Preserve which focuses on invasive exotic plant removal, exotic animal removal, hydrologic restoration and public access and stewardship. FY12 restoration activities completed by staff and volunteers include removal of feral hogs and invasive exotic plants, including Melaleuca, cogon grass, earleaf acacia and Brazilian pepper. Trail and boardwalk maintenance and volunteer lead nature tours were also conducted. Ongoing hydrologic restoration activities are being implemented adjacent to the Preserve.
Habitat_Description: Six Mile Cypress Slough Preserve is managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 and is comprised of a variety of upland and wetland plant communities including pine flatwoods, hardwood transitions, flag ponds, oak hammocks, prairie, and cypress sloughs.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This project is acquisition of 46 acres adjacent to the Charlotte Harbor Buffer Preserve (now  totaling 447 acres) for habitat and hydrologic restoration and public access and stewardship. A management plan has not been developed for the Preserve, but restoration activities focus on invasive exotic vegetation removal and prescribed fire, as well as restoration of sheet flow. The Preserve is adjacent to the state-owned Charlotte Harbor Preserve State Park and management activities are coordinated with the Florida Department of Environmental Protection.
Habitat_Description: Charlotte Harbor Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 and is comprised of pine flatwoods, scrubby flatwoods, scrub, oak hammock, tidal salt flats, tidal marsh, tidal swamp. There is widely distributed exotic vegetation including Australian pine, Melaleuca and Brazilian pepper. The diverse habitats support a wide variety of plant and animal species, including wading birds, Gopher tortoise and mammals.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a new land acquisition of the 82 acre Buttonwood Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 for preservation and restoration of native and disturbed upland, wetland and submerged estuarine habitats, including extensive mangroves and seagrasses. In the future, exotic vegetation will be removed and natural hydrology will be restored. A management plan for the preserve will be developed by Lee County Conservation 2020 which will include public education about the native habitats and restoration activities, as well as public access.
Habitat_Description: This is a new acquisition of the 82 acre Buttonwood Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. The primary habitat is mangrove wetlands along Pine Island Creek, including 45 acres of mangroves and submerged  estuarine habitats in Pine Island Creek and 92 acres of pine flatwoods and disturbed uplands. The habitats suport a variety of wildlife including wading and song birds and estuarine fishes.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 8 acre Surfside Park managed by the City of Cape Coral for ecosystem restoration and public access and environmental education. Management activities focus on invasive exotic plant removal, as well as public facilities for hiking. FY12 restoration activities completed by contractors, staff and volunteers included removal of Melaleuca, Australian pine and earleaf acacia. The work was done at no cost to the City of Cape Coral because the contractor received the wood as payment for their work. Herbicide treatment of new growth will begin in the fall of 2012 and the herbicides were provided by the Florida State Herbicide Bank. All survey work was done by the City of Cape Coral’s Environmental Resources Division.
Habitat_Description: Surfside Woods Park is managed by the City of Cape Coral and is comprised of a variety of upland habitats including pine palmetto and oak hammock, with extensive areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Melaleuca, Australian pine and earleaf acacia. The park is surrounded by residential and urban development.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This project includes exotic invasive vegetation and trash removal on 20 acres of tidal swamp mangroves and over wash berm hammocks in the Cayo Pelau Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 for habitat restoration and protection. Lee County 2020 staff and Calusa Land Trust and Bokeelia Boat Club volunteers removed Brazilian pepper, Australian pine, other non-native plants and trash from the mangroves and shell berms. The volunteers accessed the island and removed the trash via boat.
Habitat_Description: This project includes 20 acres of native and disturbed uplands and wetlands in the Cayo Pelau Preserve, an island in Charlotte Harbor managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 for habitat restoration and protection. The primary habitat of the island preserve is tidal swamp, comprised mostly of mangroves, with some shell berm with native hammock vegetation and invasive exotic vegetation, including Brazilian pepper and Australian pine. The vegetation is thick with the exception of three small beaches along the northwestern coastline.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the existing 1,727 acre Telegraph Creek Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. A management plan has been developed for the Preserve which focuses on habitat restoration and public access and stewardship. FY12 habitat restoration activities completed by staff include removal of 17 feral hogs, removal of invasive exotic plants, including Brazilian pepper and Melaleuca, enhancement of Scrub Jay and Gopher tortoise habitat and reduction of fire fuel loads in preparation for prescribed fire.
Habitat_Description: Telegraph Creek Preserve is managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 and is comprised of a variety of upland and wetland habitats, including scrub and palmetto prairie and riverine wetlands along Telegraph Creek. There is some invasive exotic vegetation, including Brazilian pepper and Melaleuca, and habitat diversity is reduced due to lack of burning. The native habitats support a wide variety of plant and animal species, including Scrub Jay, Gopher Tortoise, black bear, Florida panther, crested caracara, red-cockaded woodpecker, eastern indigo snake and burrowing owls.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: The Cocker Trust 2 Acquisition is purchase of a 38 acre parcel native mangrove and salt flat habitats on southwestern Pine Island, adjacent to the Pine Island Sound Aquatic Preserve. The parcel was purchased by the non-profit Calusa Land Trust of Pine Island for preservation and restoration. The parcel is bordered to the north and south by native mangrove habitats, to the east by salt flats, and to the west by state managed aquatic preserve with submerged seagrasses. Acquisition of the parcel prevents the area from future development. A management plan has not been developed for the parcel yet, but in the future Calusa Land Trust volunteers will conduct regular visits to the parcel to monitor the parcel for invasive exotic vegetation. Preservation of the native mangroves and salt flats protects fish and wildlife habitat and improves water quantity and quality draining to the adjacent submerged seagrass habitats.
Habitat_Description: The Coker Trust 2 Acquisition is a 38 acre parcel purchased by the Calusa Land Trust and Nature Preserve of Pine Island for preservation and restoration. The parcel is located in Lee County, on southwestern Pine Island, adjacent to the Pine Island Sound estuary. The primary habitat on the parcel is native mangrove wetlands, with a very small area of salt flats in the northwest of the parcel. The parcel borders submerged seagrasses in the adjacent estuary. The parcel has no hydrologic alteration and very little invasive exotic vegetation. The native mangroves and salt flats support a great  diversity of wading birds, including great and little blue herons, roseate spoonbills and green herons, as well as several species of crabs, raccoons, bobcats, mosquito fish, mangrove snapper and snook.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This project includes continuing habitat restoration at the existing 1,295 acre Caloosahatchee Creeks preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. Invasive exotic vegetation, including cogongrass, Guinea grass, Lygodium, Wedelia, air potato and Brazilian pepper was removed throughout the 20 acre preserve by agency staff and Department of Corrections workers, with assistance from volunteers. Roller chopping of palmetto plants, Brazilian Pepper control, and wild hog trapping were completed. Nine wild hogs were removed. A management plan is being developed for the preserve.
Habitat_Description: Caloosahatchee Creeks Preserve is managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 and is comprised of a variety of upland and wetland habitats in several parcels along the north side of the Caloosahatchee River east and West of I-75. Habitats include oak hammocks, pine flatwoods and mangroves, and extensive areas of exotic vegetation.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project in the 175 acre Gator hole preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. There are a variety of native and disturbed uplands and wetlands. Management activities  have been done to accommodate gopher tortoises relocated by Lee County transportation projects. Restoration activities include invasive exotic plant removal, roller shopping and mowing palmetto to reduce fire fuel, prescribed burning and pine tree thining, as well as fencing. The number of plant species increased by over 100 once the invasive exotic plants were removed, palmetto cover reduced and a prescribed fire program initiated. During FY 12 a  total of three prescribed burns on 90 acres of land were completed.
Habitat_Description: Gator Hole Preserve is managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 and consists primarily of wet and mesic flatwoods (72%); other natural plant communities include dome swamp, depression marsh and wet prairie. There are also disturbed communities related to historical farming on the Preserve. Over 250 plant and 120 animal species have been documented in the Preserve, including gopher tortoise, amphibians and wading birds.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This project includes acquisition of 2 acres of native and disturbed upland and wetlands adjacent to the Orange River Preserve (now totaling over 60 acres) managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 for habitat preservation and restoration and public access and education. In the future, the activities on the parcel will include treating invasive exotic vegetation, primarily Melaleuca, but including Caesar Weed, and Brazilian pepper, as well as prescribed fire. A management plan is being developed for the preserve by Lee County Conservation 2020 which will include public access and education about the native habitats and restoration activities and volunteer workdays.
Habitat_Description: This project includes acquisition of 2 acres of native and disturbed upland and wetlands adjacent to the existing Orange River Preserve (now totalling over 60 acres)managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 for habitat preservation and restoration. The habitats are comprised of three plant communities including scrubby flatwoods, mesic hammock and tidal swamp, including three species of mangroves, and apples and leather fern. There is also extensive invasive exotic vegetation including Melaleuca and Brazilian pepper.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Daniels Preserve at Spanish Creek Restoration
Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the existing 243 acre Daniels Preserve at Spanish Creek Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. The habitat restoration that includes exotic fauna and invasive exotic vegetation removal, as well as preparation for prescribed fire and restoration of native vegetation and hydrology along the headwaters of Spanish Creek. New hog trapper began trapping hogs in the preserve in September and a total of eighty-two hogs were captured and removed.
Habitat_Description: Daniels Preserve at Spanish Creek Preserve is managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 and is comprised of 21 plant communities and the headwaters of Spanish Creek. The dominant plant communities are pine flatwoods, oak hammocks, wetlands forested, mixed and pine-mesic oak, along with improved pasture that is still in an active cattle lease. There are areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Brazilian pepper and cogongrass. The native habitats support a diversity of animal species, including the listed Gopher Tortoise.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This project includes upland, wetland and Gopher tortoise habitat restoration at the 38 acre Koreshan Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. A management plan was developed for the Preserve and in the past invasive exotic vegetation was treated by contractors, invasive exotic plant species, including downy rose myrtle, Guinea grass, rosary pea and air potato. In FY12, maintenance treatment of invasive exotic vegetation was conducted and Gopher tortoise burrows were safely located, flagged and GPS’ed by staff.
Habitat_Description: Koreshan Preserve is a Lee County Conservation 2020 Preserve comprised of two main plant communities, including disturbed scrubby flatwoods and mesic hammock. These sites are classified as disturbed due to the invasive exotic plants and lack of fire. The site hosts a concentration of gopher tortoises along with a diversity of songbirds and reptiles.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a new 310 acre land acquisition adjacent to the existing Alva Scrub Preserve (now totaling 1,155 acres) managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 for preservation and restoration of habitats. In the future, invasive exotic vegetation (Lygodium, tropical soda apple, cogongrass and Brazilian pepper) will be removed, and roller chopping done in preparation for prescribed fire. A cooperative Scrub Jay mitigation plan is being developed and Scrub Jay and Gopher Tortoise habitat restoration activities have been started.
Habitat_Description: Alva Scrub Preserve addition is managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 includes a diversity of plant communities comprising mesic and scrubby flatwoods, oak hammock, wet prairie, floodplain swamp, cypress head and ponds, as well as invasive exotic vegetation including cogongrass, Lygodium, tropical soda apple, Brazilian pepper and Melaleuca. The native habitats provide feeding and roosting areas for numerous listed wading bird species, Scrub Jays, Gopher Tortoise and other animal species. Habitat diversity is decreased by lack of burning.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Charlotte Harbor Preserve State Park Port Charlotte Restoration
Project_Description: This is a an habitat restoration project at the 5,855 acre Port Charlotte Management Area of the Charlotte Harbor Preserve State Park managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. There is an approved management plan for the area and management focuses on habitat restoration and public access. Restoration activities focus on prescribed fire and removal of non-native vegetation and animals, to improve wildlife habitat. FY12 restoration activities completed included 25 acres of invasive exotic vegetation treatment of Brazilian pepper, Old World Climbing Fern,  rosary pea,  Melaleuca, and cogongrass, as well as road and trail maintenance.
Habitat_Description: The Port Charlotte Management Area (5,855 acres) of the Charlotte Harbor Preserve State Park is managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. The Port Charlotte Management Area is located along the north shore of Charlotte Harbor between the Myakka and Peace Rivers in Charlotte County. The habitats include mesic pine flatwoods, scrubby flatwoods, salt flats, salt marshes, mangrove islands, tidal creeks and numerous embayment’s. The tidal creeks include Tippecanoe, Sam Knight and Flopbuck, which drain to the estuaries and seagrasses of the Gasparilla Sound/Charlotte Harbor Aquatic Preserve. The habitats support a great diversity of wildlife, birds, fish and native plants including bob cat, bald eagle, great blue heron, snook, sea trout and manatee. The pine flatwoods have high fire fuel loads and there are extensive areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Brazilian pepper, Australian pine, Melaleuca, cogongrass, and old world climbing fern.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Sleeping Turtles Preserve North and South Restoration
Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 987 acre Sleeping Turtles Preserve North and South managed by Sarasota County. Management focuses on habitat restoration and public access. Restoration activities focus on invasive exotic vegetation removal to improve wildlife habitat. The preserve is one of the publicly-owned properties bordering the Wild and Scenic Myakka River, forever protecting a piece of the riverine floodplain. FY12 restoration activities completed by staff and volunteers included 6 acres invasive exotic vegetation removal, including Brazilian pepper, Australian pine, and Melaleuca, as well as maintenance of trails.
Habitat_Description: Sleeping Turtles Preserve North and South (987 acres) is managed by the Sarasota County Environmentally Sensitive Lands Protection Program. The preserve is located along the Myakka River, a designated Wild and Scenic River, east of Nokomis and Venice. The preserve is named after the Sleeping Turtles landmark noted on the 1800s naval maps of the Myakka River. The preserve includes a mosaic of diverse natural communities including floodplain swamps, pine flatwoods, upland mixed forests and seasonal wetlands. The habitats support a great diversity of native vegetation, wild flowers, wildlife, birds and fish, including bobcats, gopher tortoises, alligators, swallow-tailed kites, osprey, a variety of song birds, false foxglove, blazing star, pennyroyal and spider lily. There are scattered areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Brazilian pepper, Australian pines, Melaleuca and cogon grass. Trails provide public access and wildlife viewing.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 225 acre Amberjack Environmental Park managed by the Charlotte Harbor Environmental Center and Charlotte County. Management of the park focuses on habitat restoration and public access, including hiking trails and boardwalks. Restoration activities focus on removal of invasive exotic plants to improve wildlife habitat. FY12 restoration activities completed by staff and volunteers included treatment of Brazilian pepper, Java plum and Melaleuca. In addition, existing trails and boardwalks were maintained for public access to the park.
Habitat_Description: Amberjack Environmental Park (225 acres) is managed by the Charlotte Harbor Environmental Center and Charlotte County. The habitats are comprised of oak scrub, pine flatwoods, two significant freshwater wetlands which form the tributaries to the Lemon Bay Aquatic Preserve and Coral Creek, and a freshwater pond. These unique habitats are havens for several species of wading birds, including glossy ibis, roseate spoonbills and snowy egrets. They are havens for several species of wading birds, including glossy ibis, roseate spoonbills and snowy egrets. There a some areas of invasive exotic vegetation throughout the park, including Brazilian pepper, Java plum and Melaleuca. Trails, boardwalks and observational platforms provide public access and viewing of an amazing variety of birds who in habitat the park.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: The Willow Lake Wetlands Acquisition is purchase of 1 acre of highly disturbed mangrove habitat on western Pine Island, adjacent to the Pine Island Sound estuary. The parcel was purchased by the non-profit Calusa Land Trust of Pine Island for preservation, restoration and public access to conservation lands. The parcel is bordered to the north and south by privately owned mangrove habitats, to the east by high density residential mobile home community and to the west  by a state managed aquatic preserve with submerged seagrasses. Acquisition of the parcel prevents the area from future development. A management plan has not been developed for the parcel yet, but in the future Calusa Land Trust volunteers will conduct regular visits to the parcel to remove the infestation of the invasive exotic Australian Pines. Removal of the invasive exotic vegetation and restoration of the mangroves will enhance fish and wildlife habitat and improve water quantity and quality draining to the adjacent submerged seagrass habitats. Primary access to the parcel by volunteers and the public will be via canoe, kayak and shallow draft boat.
Habitat_Description: The Willow Lake Wetlands Acquisition is a 1 acre parcel purchased by the Calusa Land Trust and Nature Preserve of Pine Island for preservation and restoration. The parcel is located in Lee County, on western Pine Island, adjacent to Pine Island Sound. The primary habitat is highly disturbed and native mangrove wetlands bordering submerged seagrasses in the adjacent estuary. The parcel has extensive hydrologic alteration and invasive exotic vegetation, primarily Australian pines, associated with berms made from spoil from past dredging of the adjacent channel. The native mangroves support a wide diversity of wading birds, including great blue herons, black crown night herons and white ibis, invertebrates including mud and mangrove tree crabs, and fisheries including  mosquito fish, mangrove snapper and snook.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Garden of Five Senses Park Native Plantings
Project_Description: This is a native vegetation planting project at the 16 acre Garden of Five Senses park managed by the City of North Port. A management plan has been developed for the park which focus on public education about Florida native vegetation, wildlife, birds and butterflies. The park will be develop in 3 phases and provide educational and recreational opportunities. The butterfly garden and native plant walk have been completed on 4 acres of the park property. The native plantings, trails and signs reach an essential target audience and provide critical demonstration to local residents about the value of protecting and restoring diverse native habitats.
Habitat_Description: Garden of Five Senses park is managed by the City of North Port and is a 12 acre “urban pocket park” surrounded by moderate density residential land use. The primary native habitats are small areas of pine flatwoods and oak hammocks, with large areas of disturbed, open grassy fields that are being restored to native vegetation. The Florida Friendly plantings of native trees, shrubs and wildflowers include oak, slash pine, beauty berry, wild coffee, lantana, buttonwood, stopper, porter weed, fire bush and milkweed. The plantings provide an oasis for wildlife, birds and butterflies along a winding path used for public education about native Florida habitats.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: The Inman Slagle Acquisition is purchase of a 20 acre parcel of moderately disturbed mangrove habitat on northwestern western Pine Island, adjacent to the Pine Island Sound Aquatic Preserve and Smoke House Bay Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. The parcel was purchased by the non-profit Calusa Land Trust of Pine Island for preservation, restoration and public access to conservation lands. The parcel is bordered to the north and south by moderately disturbed mangrove habitats, to the east by low density residential and agricultural land use and to the west by state managed aquatic preserve with submerged seagrasses. Acquisition of the parcel prevents the area from future development. A management plan has not been developed for the parcel yet, but in the future Calusa Land Trust volunteers will conduct regular visits to the parcel to remove the infestation of the invasive exotic Australian Pines and Brazilian and will consider hydrologic restoration activities. Removal of the invasive exotic vegetation and restoration of the mangroves will enhance fish and wildlife habitat and improve water quantity and quality draining to the adjacent submerged seagrass habitats. Primary access to the parcel by volunteers and the public will be via canoe, kayak and shallow draft boat.
Habitat_Description: The Inman Slagle Acquisition is a 20 acre parcel purchased by the Calusa Land Trust and Nature Preserve of Pine Island for preservation and restoration. The parcel is located in Lee County, on northwestern Pine Island, adjacent to the Pine Island Sound estuary and the Smokehouse Bay Preserve, currently under restoration by Lee County Conservation 2020. The primary habitat on the parcel is moderately disturbed and native mangrove wetlands bordering submerged seagrasses in the adjacent estuary. The parcel has extensive hydrologic alteration from past mosquito control ditching and moderate levels of invasive exotic vegetation, including Australian pine and Brazilian pepper on the spoil piles adjacent to the ditches. The native mangroves support a wide diversity of mammals, including raccoons and bob cat, wading birds, including little blue and night herons, invertebrates including mud and mangrove tree crabs, and fisheries including mosquito fish, mangrove snapper and snook.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 115 acre Cedar Point Environmental Park managed by the Charlotte Harbor Environmental Center and Charlotte County. Management of the preserve focuses on habitat restoration and public access, including hiking trails. Restoration activities focus on removal of invasive exotic plants to improve wildlife habitat. FY12 restoration activities completed by staff and volunteers included treatment of Brazilian pepper, Java plum and Melaleuca. In addition, existing trails were maintained for public access to the park.
Habitat_Description: Cedar Point Environmental Park (115+ acres) is managed by the Charlotte Harbor Environmental Center and Charlotte County and is a peninsula between Lemon Bay Aquatic Preserve, Oyster Creek and Ainger Creek in Englewood. The habitats are comprised mostly of mesic and xeric pine flatwoods, with additional scrub, coastal strand, hydric pine, high marsh and fringing mangrove wetlands. These upland and wetland habitats are adjacent to submerged seagrass habitats in the estuary. The habitats support a great diversity of wildlife, birds, fish and invertebrates, including gopher tortoises, bald eagle, osprey, crabs, native wildflowers, bait fish species and mangrove snapper. There are some areas of invasive exotic vegetation, including Brazilian pepper, Java plum and Melaleuca. Trails provide public access and wildlife viewing throughout the park.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Paynes Creek Historic State Park Restoration
Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 396  acre Paynes Creek Historic State Park managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. There is an approved management plan for the park and management focuses on habitat and hydrologic restoration and public access. Restoration activities focus on prescribed fire and removal of non-native vegetation and animals, to improve wildlife habitat. FY12 restoration activities completed included 19 acres of prescribed fire, as well as exotic plant and animal removal and trail maintenance.
Habitat_Description: Paynes Creek Historic State Park (396 acres) is managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection and is located at confluence of Paynes Creek and the Peace River in Hardee County. A mosaic of 10 upland and wetland habitats occur in the park, including mesic flatwoods, sandhill, scrub, scrubby flatwoods, xeric hammock, baygall, bottomland forest, floodplain swamp, hydric hammock, blackwater stream, and seepage stream, as well as old pasture lands. The habitats support a great diversity of native plants, mammals, birds and reptiles including longleaf and sand pine, scrub and turkey oak, wax myrtle, river otter, black bear, Florida gopher frog and box turtle, wood duck, and swallow-tailed kite. The pine flatwoods have heavy fire fuel loads, invasive exotic vegetation is a problem, especially on the old pasture lands and includes tropical soda apple, cogongrass, world climbing fern, air potato, and hydrilla.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the existing 307 acre Pop Ash Creek Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. A management plan has been completed for the Preserve which focuses on habitat and hydrologic restoration and public stewardship and access, including hiking, fishing, birding and horseback riding. FY12 restoration activities completed by staff and volunteers included removal of earleaf acacia, Caesar weed, cogongrass, Guinea grass Melaleuca and Brazilian pepper. Work continued on the hydrologic restoration activities to correct historic sheet flow into the preserve, connect artificial ponds and reduce flooding in the adjacent neighborhoods.
Habitat_Description: Pop Ash Creek Preserve is managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 and is comprised of wet and mesic pine flatwoods and riverine wetlands, as well as invasive exotic vegetation including ear leaf acacia, cogongrass, Carolina willow, Brazilian pepper, and Melaleuca. A portion of the blackwater stream Popash Creek is within the preserve and hydrology within and draining to the preserve has been extensively altered, affecting 90% of the preserve.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 100 acre Myakka Island Point Preserve managed by Sarasota County. Management focuses on habitat restoration and public access. Restoration activities focus on invasive exotic vegetation removal to improve wildlife habitat. The preserve is one of the publicly-owned properties bordering the Wild and Scenic Myakka River, forever protecting a piece of the riverine floodplain. FY12 restoration activities completed by county staff and volunteers included removal of 5 acres of Brazilian pepper, Australian pine, Melaleuca and cogongrass.
Habitat_Description: Myakka Island Point Preserve (100 acres) is managed by the Sarasota County Environmentally Sensitive Lands Protection Program. The preserve is located along the Myakka River, a designated Wild and Scenic River, north of Port Charlotte. The native habitats include the Myakka River, tidal salt marsh, tidal mangrove swamp, scrubby pine flatwoods, tropical hammock and slash pine flatwoods. The habitats support a great diversity of wildlife, birds, fish and native plants, including snook, American kestrels, swallow-tailed kites, and a variety of wading birds, amphibians and wetland plants. Invasive exotic vegetation including Brazilian pepper, Australian pine, Melaleuca and cogon grass occurs throughout the preserve. Trails provide public access and wildlife viewing.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a new land acquisition of 43.5 acres adjacent to the existing Pine Lake Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 for restoration of habitat and hydrology, as well as public access and community stewardship. A management plan has been developed for the Pine Lake Preserve which focuses on habitat and hydrologic restoration. This new acquisition will allow further protection and restoration of tributaries to the Imperial River and will help improve water quality, rehydrate adjacent wetlands and reduce future flooding.
Habitat_Description: Pine Lake Preserve Acquisition is a new 43.5 acre purchase adjacent to the existing Pine Lake Preserve is managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. The parcel is comprised of native and disturbed cypress-pine communities, pine flatwoods and oak hammocks, with some grassy fields and extensive invasive exotic vegetation (primarily Melaleuca), as well as hydrologic alterations and a borrow pit. The native habitats provide habitat for a number of wading birds including herons, egrets, sandpipers, killdeer and black-neck stilts. The preserve is located along the Imperial River floodplain and is surrounded by residential and urban development that has altered the hydrology. Lack of burning has reduced habitat diversity and increased fire fuel loads.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Six Mile Cypress North Preserve Restoration
Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project in the 1,219 acre Six Mile Cypress North Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. A management plan has not yet been developed for the Preserve, but ongoing restoration activities focus on habitat and hydrologic restoration. The Department of Transportation will be constructing a wildlife crossing under an adjacent road when it is widened. There are currently no public access activities at the Preserve. FY12 restoration activities completed by staff include removal of exotic vegetation, primarily Brazilian pepper, throughout the Preserve.
Habitat_Description: Six Mile Cypress North Preserve is managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 and is comprised of pine flatwoods, oak hammocks, cypress sloughs, riverine wetlands, abandoned agriculture fields and the historic headwaters of the Six Mile Cypress Slough. The native uplands, wetlands and agricultural lands include invasive exotic vegetation and have altered hydrology within and into the preserve. The diverse habitats are utilizes by a wide variety of wildlife and bird species.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 80 acre Curry Creek Preserve managed by Sarasota County. Management of the preserve focuses on habitat restoration and public access, though hydrologic restoration is being conducted in the adjacent preserve managed by Sarasota County Public Works which will also help with habitat restoration in the preserve. Restoration activities focus on removal of invasive exotic plant removal to improve wildlife habitat. FY12 restoration activities completed by staff and volunteers included removal and/or treatment of Brazilian pepper, Australian pine and Melaleuca.
Habitat_Description: Curry Creek Preserve (80 acres) is managed by Sarasota County and is located along Curry Creek, a tributary to Dona and Roberts Bays in Venice. The preserve is adjacent to a 19 acre Sarasota County Public works tidal marsh and swamp restoration site, as well as a high residential community. The native habitats at the preserve include mangrove forests, tidal marshes and scrub and pine flatwoods. Pond apple trees, a rarity in Sarasota County, can be found in forested areas upstream along the creek. The habitats support a wide variety of wildlife, birds and fish, including gopher tortoises, alligators, river otters, eastern indigo snakes and an assortment of wading birds such as the roseate spoonbill and wood stork. Trails throughout the preserve provide public access and wildlife viewing. There are small areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Brazilian pepper, Australian pine and Melaleuca.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 6,439 acre Deer Prairie Creek Preserve managed jointly by Sarasota County and the Southwest Florida Water Management District. Management of the preserve focuses on habitat restoration and public access. Restoration activities focus on prescribed fire and removal of feral hogs and invasive exotic vegetation to improve wildlife habitat. FY12 restoration activities completed by staff, contractors and volunteers included 952 acres of prescribed fire, 20 acres of Brazilian pepper, Australian Pine, Melaleuca and cogon grass treatment and feral hog removal. Cost estimates are for Sarasota County contributions to prescribed fire only.
Habitat_Description: Deer Prairie Creek Preserve (6,439 acres) is managed by the Sarasota County Environmentally Sensitive Lands Protection Program and Southwest Florida Water Management District. The Preserve is located along Deer Prairie Creek and the Myakka River, a designated Wild and Scenic River, west of Venice. The native habitats include pine flatwoods, prairie hammock and seasonal wetlands. A variety of wildlife species inhabit the preserve including gopher tortoises, alligators, river otter, wild turkey, swallow-tailed kite, Florida scrub-jays and an assortment of wading birds. Native flowering plants, such as St. John’s wort, tarflower and pine lily thrive throughout the landscape, with particularly striking displays during the spring and fall. Trails throughout the preserve provide public access and wildlife viewing. The native uplands have heavy fire fuel loads and there are widely distributed areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Brazilian pepper, Australian pine, Melaleuca and cogongrass.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: East Mullock Drainage District Habitat Restoration
Project_Description: The native planting component of the East Mullock Drainage District Habitat Restoration Project is managed by a professor at Florida Gulf Coast University. The site is located along a drainage ditch with steep side slopes that leads to the headwaters of Mullock Creek, which is a tributary to Estero Bay. The adjacent land use is residential and the watershed has highly altered habitats and hydrology. A significant portion of the invasive exotic vegetation was removed and the slopes was stabilized and mulched in 2009. Since that time, appropriate native vegetation has been planted in phases along the shoreline by volunteers from Florida Gulf Coast University and the local community. The native species, chosen for their drought and sun tolerance, stabilize the bank slopes, provide habitat for fish and wildlife, and filter stormwater runoff. In FY12, volunteers planted native species include button bush, cypress, wax myrtle, Myrsine, Dahoon holly, green buttonwood, fiddlewood, seagrape, sea oxeye daisy and white indigo berry, along 300 feet of shoreline upslope to a width of 15 feet, as well as continued to remove invasive exotic vegetation that resprouted
Habitat_Description: The East Mullock Drainage District Habitat Restoration Project site is located in Lee County and is comprised of a highly disturbed steep bank of an artificial drainage ditch leading to Mullock Creek and surrounded by a residential community with highly altered habitats and hydrology. Unrestored areas of the site have extensive invasive exotic vegetation, including Brazilian pepper, air potato and non-native grasses. Restored areas have native vegetation species including button bush, cypress, wax myrtle, Myrsine, Dahoon holly, green buttonwood, fiddlewood, seagrape, sea oxeye daisy and white indigo berry.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: The Cocker Trust 1 Acquisition is a purchase of 40 acres of undisturbed mangrove habitat on southeastern Pine Island, adjacent to the Matlacha Pass estuary. The parcel was purchased by the non-profit Calusa Land Trust of Pine Island for preservation, restoration and public access to conservation lands. The parcel is surrounded by privately owned mangrove habitats, adjacent to low density residential land use to the west and state managed submerged aquatic preserve to the east. Acquisition of the healthy mangrove wetlands prevents the area from future development and maintains the diversity of habitats and water quantity and quality draining to the adjacent submerged seagrass habitats. A management plan has not been developed for the parcel yet, but in the future Calusa Land Trust volunteers will conduct regular visits to the parcel to remove what limited invasive exotic vegetation there is. Primary access to the parcel by volunteers and the public will be via canoe, kayak and shallow draft boat.
Habitat_Description: The Cocker Trust 1 Acquisition is a 40 acre parcel purchased by the Calusa Land Trust and Nature Preserve of Pine Island for preservation and restoration. The parcel is located in Lee County, on southeastern Pine Island, adjacent to Matlacha Pass. The sole habitat is undisturbed native mangrove wetlands bordering submerged seagrasses in the adjacent estuary. The parcel has no hydrologic alterations and little invasive exotic vegetation and supports a wide diversity of saltwater and estuarine invertebrate, bird and mammal species including white ibis, black crowned night herons, mud crabs, mangrove tree crabs, white ibis, mangrove snapper, and raccoons.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Charlotte Harbor Preserve State Park Cape Haze Restoration
Project_Description: This is a an habitat restoration project at the 20,343 acre Cape Haze Management Area of the Charlotte Harbor Preserve State Park managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. There is an approved management plan for the area and management focuses on habitat restoration and public access. Restoration activities focus on prescribed fire and removal of non-native vegetation and animals, to improve wildlife habitat. FY12 restoration activities completed included 207 acres of prescribed fire and 179 acres of invasive exotic vegetation treatment of Brazilian pepper, Melaleuca, Australian pine and cogon, torpedo and natal grass, as well as road and trail maintenance.
Habitat_Description: The Cape Haze Management Area (20,343) of the Charlotte Harbor Preserve State Park is managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection.
