The Cape Haze Management Area is located along the west shore of Charlotte Harbor in Charlotte County. The habitats include pine flatwoods, oak scrub, tropical hammock midden/mound, freshwater and salt marshes, mangrove islands and tidal creeks. The tidal creeks include Catfish, Widden, Sisters Pond, Trout and Big Muddy, which drain to the estuaries and seagrasses of the Gasparilla Sound/Charlotte Harbor and Cape Haze Aquatic Preserve. The habitats support a great diversity of wildlife, birds, fish and native plants including panther, bald eagle, great blue heron, snook, sea trout and gumbo limbo. The pine flatwoods have high fire fuel loads and there are extensive areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Brazilian pepper, Australian pine, Melaleuca, cogongrass, and old world climbing fern.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 6,151 acre Pinelands Reserve managed by Sarasota County. Management focuses on habitat restoration and protection. Restoration activities focus on prescribed fire and  invasive exotic animal and vegetation removal to improve wildlife habitat. FY12 restoration activities completed by Sarasota County and Florida Department of Forestry staff included 1,097 acres of prescribed fire, 11 acres of roller chopping to reduce fire fuel loads, removal of 94 feral hogs and 20 acres of invasive exotic species, including Brazilian pepper, Australian pine, Melaleuca and cogongrass. Cost estimates are for Sarasota County contributions to prescribed fire only.
Habitat_Description: The Pinelands Reserve (6,151 acres) is managed by Sarasota County for multiple purposes including protecting native habitats and buffering the construction of a county solid waste disposal site. The site is located between Shackett Creek and Cow Pen Slough east of Sarasota and Nokomis. The native habitats include pine flatwoods, upland mixed forests, lakes and seasonal wetlands. The habitats support a diversity of wildlife and song and wading birds, including bob cat, gopher tortoises, bald eagles, roseate spoonbills, great crested caracara and swallow-tailed kites. The pine flatwoods have a heavy fire fuel load and there is extensive invasive exotic vegetation, including Brazilian pepper, Australian pine, Melaleuca, cogongrass, Ludwigia and tropical soda apple. Public access to the site is limited to a perimeter road and guided hiking tours only.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 130 acre Pine Lake Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. A management plan has been developed for the Preserve which focuses on habitat and hydrologic restoration, as well as public access. FY12 restoration activities included the completion of removal of cabbage palms, roller chopping and fireline widening in preparation for prescribed fire, as well as ongoing removal of invasive exotic vegetation including Melaleuca. Future hydrologic restoration, hiking, bird watching and nature study activities are being planned.
Habitat_Description: Pine Lake Preserve is managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 and is comprised of cypress-pine communities, pine flatwoods, oak hammocks and riverine floodplain, with extensive invasive exotic vegetation (primarily Melaleuca), as well as hydrologic alterations, including a large borrow pit. The native habitats and borrow bit provide habitat for a number of wading birds including herons, egrets, sandpipers, killdeer and black-neck stilts, as well as American alligators. The preserve is located along the Imperial River floodplain. Lack of burning has reduced habitat diversity and increased fire fuel loads.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This project includes habitat restoration at the existing 730 acre Pine Island Flatwoods Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. A management plan has been developed for the Preserve which focuses on habitat restoration and public stewardship and access. During FY12, contractors, staff and volunteers from Lee County Conservation 2020 and Calusa Land trust completed roller chopping of 15 acres of palmettos, logging of Melaleuca, removing other invasive exotic plants, planting long leaf and slash pines and trail maintenance.
Habitat_Description: Pine Island Flatwood Preserve is managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 and is comprised of nine plant communities including mesic pine flatwoods, freshwater marshes, tidal swamp, hydric hammock, coastal grassland, coastal berm, improved pastures and abandoned groves. The area has exotic vegetation including Melaleuca and Brazilian pepper and high fire fuel loads. The habitats support a variety of wildlife including Gopher Tortoise, wading birds and small mammals. The southern portion of the Preserve is bordered by Stringfellow Road to the east, and mangrove swamp and mudflats to the west.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This project includes habitat and hydrologic restoration at the existing 272 acre Deep Lagoon Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. There are extensive invasive exotic plant mono-cultures of Australian pines, Brazilian pepper and melaleuca and hydrologic alterations within and into the preserve, which is surrounded by urbanized development. The preserve is in several parcels with a small area along the Caloosahatchee River. Staff and volunteers removed invasive exotic plants, including Australian Pines, Melaleuca and Brazilian pepper through cutting and herbicide treatments, graded previous agriculture lands to restore hydrology and natural flows removed trash, dangerous debris and monofilament fishing line
Habitat_Description: Deep Lagoon Preserve is managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 and is comprised of tidal swamps and marshes, coastal grasslands, wet prairies and prairie hammocks and mesic flatwoods, as well as pasture and old gladiolus agriculture fields. There are extensive invasive exotic plant mono-cultures of Australian pines, Brazilian pepper and melaleuca and hydrologic alterations within and into the preserve, which is surrounded by urbanized development. The native habitats support a variety of other plant and animal species, including several listed species, including the Smalltooth Sawfish. The preserve is in several parcels with a small area along the Caloosahatchee River.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This is a very small habitat and hydrologic project at the 2 acre Lake Martha Lakefront site managed by the City of Winter Haven. The city has adopted the Chain of Lakes Water Quality Management Plan to increase water infiltration areas, restore natural habitats and create green space throughout the city. FY12 restoration activities at the Lake Marion Lakefront site included removing invasive exotic vegetation and enhancing native vegetation in the stormwater swale and along the lake shoreline.
Habitat_Description: The Lake Martha Lakefront site (2 acres) is managed by the City of Winter Haven. The site is located along the northeast shore of Lake Martha, surrounded by high density residential area and adjacent to the baseball field. The site receives runoff from the local watershed. There are some native pines and oaks on the site, as well as some invasive exotic vegetation, including Australian Pine, with the majority of the site being mowed grass, leading to emergent and submerged aquatic vegetation along the lake shore. The hydrology to the site is altered and there is a stormwater swale and paved boat ramp at the site.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: This project includes habitat restoration at the existing Alva Scrub Preserve (now totaling 1,115 acres) managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. Invasive exotic vegetation was treated and/or removed, including cogongrass, guinea grass Lygodium, tropical soda apple, and Brazilian pepper. Roller chopping was completed and 2 prescribed fires were carried out in 2 units of the preserve. Scrub Jay mitigation plan is being developed and Scrub Jay and Gopher Tortoise habitat restoration activities have been started.
Habitat_Description: Alva Scrub Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020 comprised of a diversity of plant communities including mesic and scrubby flatwoods, oak hammock, wet prairie, floodplain swamp, cypress head and ponds, as well as invasive exotic vegetation including cogongrass, Lygodium, tropical soda apple, Brazilian pepper and Melaleuca. Areas of the preserve are also in unimproved pasture use with active cattle leases. The native habitats provide feeding and roosting areas for numerous listed wading bird species, Scrub Jays, Gopher Tortoise and other animal species. Habitat diversity is decreased by lack of burning.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Yucca Pens Wildlife Management Unit Prescribed Burn
Project_Description: Habitat restoration activities focus on prescribed fire, roller chopping, removal of non-native vegetation and animals and fencing, to restore natural habitats and hydrology, improve wildlife habitat and provide recreational opportunities. Over 300 acres of prescribed fire and 752 acres of roller chopping were completed, as well as invasive exotic plant and animal removal, and road and trail maintenance.
Habitat_Description: The Yucca Pens Wildlife Management Unit (14,577 acres) of the Babcock/Webb Wildlife Management Area is managed by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission. The Yucca Pens Wildlife Management Unit is located in southwestern Charlotte County and northwestern Lee County within the Charlotte Harbor watershed. The habitats include primarily hydric and mesic pine flatwoods, with some freshwater marsh and oak scrub. The habitats support a great diversity of wildlife, birds, fish and native plants including Florida black bear, bob cat, coyote, otter, eagle, osprey, wild turkeys, great blue heron, mosquitofish and killifish, as well as invasive exotic feral hogs. There are moderate areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Brazilian pepper, Australian pine, Melaleuca, cogongrass, and old world climbing fern. Illegal ATV use throughout the Yucca Pens Wildlife Management Unit created extensive trails which act as artificial ditches and caused widespread hydrologic changes from natural sheet flow to channelized flow. The ATV trails are being reduced through fencing, posting and hydrologic restoration activities.
Main_Funding_Source: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
Lead_Implementer: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Cape Haze Management Area Prescribed Fire
Project_Description: This is a an habitat restoration project at the 20,343 acre Cape Haze Management Area of the Charlotte Harbor Preserve State Park managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. Habitat restoration activities focus on prescribed fire and removal of non-native vegetation and animals, to improve species diversity and wildlife habitat. FY13 habitat restoration activities completed included 210 acres of prescribed fire, as well as feral hog and invasive exotic vegetation removal and road and trail maintenance.
Habitat_Description: The Cape Haze Management Area (20,343) of the Charlotte Harbor Preserve State Park is managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. The Cape Haze Management Area is located in the Cape Haze Peninsula between Charlotte Harbor and Gasparilla Sound in western Charlotte County. The tidal creeks include Catfish, Widden, Sisters Pond, Trout and Big Muddy, which drain to the estuaries and seagrasses of the Gasparilla Sound/Charlotte Harbor and Cape Haze Aquatic Preserve. The habitats include pine flatwoods, oak scrub, tropical hammock midden/mound, freshwater and salt marshes, mangrove islands and tidal creeks. The habitats support a great diversity of wildlife, birds, fish and native plants including panther, bald eagle, great blue heron, snook, sea trout and gumbo limbo. The pine flatwoods have high fire fuel loads and there are extensive areas of invasive exotic vegetation including melaleuca, cogon grass, guinea grass, Brazilian pepper and old world climbing fern. The Management Area is managed for habitat protection and restoration and public access.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: J. N. Ding Darling National Wildlife Refuge Prescribed Burn
Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 6,406 acre J.N. “Ding” Darling National Wildlife Refuge managed by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service. Habitat restoration activities focus on prescribed fire, removal of invasive exotic and native vegetation and hydrologic restoration to restore the diversity of natural habitats throughout the refuge ridge and swale system. FY13 restoration activities completed included 33 acres of prescribed burn to reduce fuel loads and restore diversity of species,
Habitat_Description: The J. N. “Ding” Darling National Wildlife Refuge (6,406 acres) is managed by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service. The refuge is located in western Lee County on Sanibel Island adjacent to Pine Island Sound Aquatic Preserve. One third of the refuge (2,619 acres) is designated as Wilderness Area. The refuge is a series of ridge and swales made up of several habitat types including estuarine habitat with open water, seagrass beds, mud flats and mangrove islands and interior freshwater habitats with open water ponds and spartina saltmarsh in the swales and West Indian hardwood hammocks on the ridges. Two brackish water impoundments totaling 800 acres are used extensively by wading birds and other water birds. The refuge has a large diversity of species. Several threatened and endangered species benefit from the habitats including eastern indigo snakes, American alligators, American crocodiles, wood storks, Florida manatees, Atlantic loggerhead sea turtles, Atlantic green sea turtles, hawksbill sea turtles, Kemp’s Ridley sea turtles, leatherback sea turtles, piping plovers, and smalltooth sawfish. Approximately 272 bird species have been identified utilizing refuge habitats, as well as 60 species of reptiles and amphibians, 33 species of mammals, and 102 species of fish.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: The Coker Trust 3 Acquisition is the purchase of a 20 acre parcel of native mangrove and low and high marsh habitats on northwestern Pine Island, adjacent to the Matlacha Pass Aquatic Preserve. The parcel was purchased by the non-profit Calusa Land Trust of Pine Island for preservation and restoration. Acquisition of the parcel prevents the area from future development. Preservation of the native mangroves and low and high marsh protects fish and wildlife habitat and improves water quantity and quality draining to the adjacent submerged seagrass habitats.
Habitat_Description: The Coker Trust 3 Acquisition is a 20 acre parcel purchased by the Calusa Land Trust and Nature Preserve of Pine Island for preservation and restoration. The parcel is located in Lee County, on northeastern Pine Island, adjacent to Matlacha Pass. The primary habitat is undisturbed native mangrove wetlands bordering submerged seagrasses in the adjacent estuary. About 30% of the site is moderately disturbed low and high marsh with altered hydrology due to a historic mosquito control ditch. There is a small amount of invasive exotic vegetation, primarily Brazilian pepper, and the site supports a wide diversity of saltwater and estuarine invertebrate, bird and mammal species including white ibis, black crowned night herons, mud crabs, mangrove tree crabs, white ibis, mangrove snapper, bobcats and raccoons.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Port Charlotte Management Unit Invasive Vegetation and Animal Control
Project_Description: This is a an habitat restoration project at the 5,855 acre Port Charlotte Management Area of the Charlotte Harbor Preserve State Park managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. Habitat restoration activities focus on removal of non-native vegetation and animals to improve species diversity and wildlife habitat. FY13 habitat restoration activities completed included removal of 117 acres of invasive exotic vegetation, including melaleuca, Australian pine, carrotwood and rosary pea and 6 feral hogs, as well as road and trail maintenance.
Habitat_Description: The Port Charlotte Management Area (5,855 acres) of the Charlotte Harbor Preserve State Park is managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. The Port Charlotte Management Area is located along the north shore of Charlotte Harbor between the Myakka and Peace Rivers in central Charlotte County. The tidal creeks include Tippecanoe, Sam Knight and Flopbuck, which drain to the estuaries and seagrasses of the Gasparilla Sound/Charlotte Harbor Aquatic Preserve. The habitats include mesic pine flatwoods, scrubby flatwoods, salt flats, salt marshes, mangrove islands, tidal creeks and numerous embayments. The habitats support a great diversity of wildlife, birds, fish and native plants including bob cat, bald eagle, great blue heron, snook, sea trout and manatee. The pine flatwoods have high fire fuel loads and there are extensive areas of invasive exotic vegetation including melaleuca, Australian pine, carrotwood and rosary pea. The Management Area is managed for habitat protection and restoration and public access.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Wingate Creek State Park Invasive Animal Control
Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 615 acre Wingate Creek State Park managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. Habitat restoration activities focus on prescribed fire and removal of non-native vegetation and animals, to improve species diversity and wildlife habitat. Fourteen feral hogs were removed, and a prescribed burn and trail maintenance was conducted.
Habitat_Description: Wingate Creek State Park (615 acres) is managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection and is located in eastern Manatee County along Wingate Cree, a tributary to the Myakka River. Native vegetation includes longleaf pine, slash pine, sand pine, turkey oak, myrtle oak, rosemary, tarflower, wild olive, baygall, sweet gum and many others. The habitats support a great diversity of wildlife, birds and fish including bob cat, snapping and mud turtles, wood stork, sandhill crane, roseate spoonbill, cypress, oak and wildflowers. The pine flatwoods have heavy fire fuel loads and there are high numbers of feral hogs, and extensive areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Brazilian pepper, cogongrass, climbing fern, West Indian marsh grass, water hyacinth and rosary pea. The park is managed for habitat protection and restoration, as well as public access and recreation.

Project_Description: The Peaceful Horse Ranch acquisition is 4,171 acres of diverse native uplands and wetland along the confluence of the Peace River and Horse Creek. The parcel was purchased by Mosaic for permanent conservation as required by a court settlement between Mosaic, Sierra Club and the United States Army Corps of Engineers. Acquisition of the parcel for permanent conservation prevents the area from future development and protects existing high quality natural habitats and future water quality and supply in the rivers and receiving estuary. The managing entity of the parcel may change in the future, to allow additional resource management and public access activities, but the conservation status is in perpetuity.
Habitat_Description: Peaceful Horse Ranch (4,171 acres) is located in southwestern DeSoto County at the confluence of the Peace River and Horse Creek. The parcel includes about 7 miles of the Peace River, 4 miles of Horse Creek and Aurin and Oxbow Lakes. The rivers and creeks are essential components of the region’s natural systems, flood protection, water quality and water quantity. About one third of the parcel is upland and the remainder is wetland. The natural habitats include a diverse mix of palmetto prairie, scrub oak, pine flatwoods, cypress depressional marshes and bottomland, as well as agriculture and residential uses. The habitats support many species of fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals, including many listed species. Species include bald eagle, gopher tortoise, sandhill crane, fox squirrel, scrub Jay, red-cockaded woodpecker, panther and black bear. The parcel has been on the Florida Forever list for several years as a potential acquisition to preserve the diverse natural systems as well as the water quality in the Peace River, its tributaries and Charlotte Harbor. The parcel was purchased by Mosaic in December 2012 and must remain permanently in conservation use as the result of a recent court settlement between Mosaic, Sierra Club and the United States Army Corps of Engineers. The managing entity of the parcel may change in the future, to allow additional resource management and public access activities, but the conservation status is in perpetuity.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Lemon Bay is designated as the Lemon Bay Aquatic Preserve and is managed to protect and restore submerged habitats, including seagrass, fish and shellfish. Bay scallop populations declined in the 1960s, primarily due to over harvest. Recovery of bay scallop populations requires adequate sources of larvae, especially following red tide events. Over 2 million bay scallop larvae, collected from nearshore waters in the Florida Panhandle, were released into Lemon Bay over healthy seagrass beds just prior to the stage in their life cycle where they settle onto the seagrass and develop into juvenile scallops. The purpose of the larval release was to provide adequate numbers of juvenile scallops to grow to adulthood and spawn the following fall in Lemon Bay. Monitoring of adult populations and next year’s recruitment of larvae is planned. The project involved local, state and regional agencies, as well as volunteers.
Habitat_Description: Lemon Bay (approximately 7,700 acres) is located in western Charlotte and Lee Counties between the mainland and a series of barrier islands. Lemon Bay is connected to the Gulf of Mexico through Stump and Little Gasparilla Passes. It is designated as the Lemon Bay Aquatic Preserve. It is a narrow, shallow estuary with a large percent of shoreline in mangrove habitat and a moderately developed watershed. Lemon Bay supports over 3,800 acres of seagrasses including turtle grass, shoal grass and manatee grass. The submerged habitats support a great diversity of fish, shellfish, invertebrates and marine mammals including oyster, clams, shrimp, mangrove snapper, snook, dolphins and manatees. Historically, bay scallops were abundant in Lemon Bay, but populations declined dramatically after the 1960s due to primarily to overharvesting. Seagrass and water quality conditions are adequate to support bay scallop populations, but sources of larvae are limited and red tide adversely impacts fledgling populations.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

The native vegetation species include cabbage palm, sea oats, live oaks, coontie, tallowwood, prickly pear, red mangroves, black mangroves, saltgrass, and saltwart. The habitats support a great diversity of wildlife, birds and fish including bob cat, alligator, great blue heron, osprey, snook, snapper and tarpon. The pine flatwoods have heavy fire fuel loads and there are high numbers of feral hogs, and extensive areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Brazilian pepper, Australian pine, lead tree and air potato. The park has several archaeological and historical sites. The park is managed for habitat protection and restoration, as well as public access and recreation, including hiking, camping, fishing and kayaking.

Habitat_Description: The Smith Donation Acquisition is a 0.4 acre parcel donated to the Calusa Land Trust and Nature Preserve of Pine Island for preservation and restoration. The parcel is located in Lee County, on southeastern Pine Island, adjacent to the mangrove wetlands bordering Matlacha Pass. The parcel is adjacent to the existing Calusa Land Trust St. James Creek Preserve. The primary habitat is highly disturbed upland berms adjacent to an old residential canal, bordering native mangrove wetlands adjacent the estuary. The parcel has extensive hydrologic alteration and invasive exotic vegetation, primarily Australian pines, associated with berms made from spoil from past dredging of the adjacent channel. The adjacent native mangroves support a wide diversity of wading birds, including great blue herons, black crown night herons and white ibis, invertebrates including mud and mangrove tree crabs, and fisheries including mosquito fish, mangrove snapper and snook, and mammals including otter and bobcat.

A mosaic of 15 native upland and wetland habitats occur in the park including shell mound, wet flatwoods, tidal marsh, estuarine tidal swamp/forest, coastal rock barren, coastal berm, maritime hammock, mesic flatwoods, prairie hammock, depression marsh, scrub, scrubby flatwoods, wet prairie, strand swamp, as well as ruderal and developed lands. The native vegetation species include gumbo-limbo, slash pine, cypress, spikerush, golden leather fern, red mangroves, black mangroves, wax myrtle, gallberry, live oak, myrtle oak, tarflower, and many species of wildflower, as well as seagrasses in the adjacent estuary. Project_Name: Matlacha Pass National Wildlife Refuge Invasive Vegetation Control
Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 564 acre Matlacha Pass National Wildlife Refuge managed by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service as part of the J.N. “Ding” Darling National Wildlife Refuge. Habitat restoration activities focus on removal of non-native vegetation from the refuge islands. The habitat restoration projects improve wildlife habitat within refuge islands, as well as protect submerged seagrass habitats in the adjacent estuary. Endangered and threatened species which also benefit from the habitat restoration and protection include bald eagles and wood storks, sea turtles, and manatees. FY13 restoration activities completed included 6 acres of exotic invasive vegetation removal and native vegetation planting. Exotic invasive vegetation, including Australian pine, Brazilian pepper, earleaf acacia, papaya, seaside mahoe, lead tree, and beach naupaka were mechanically cut, removed and burned. Native species planted included black mangrove, red mangrove, black bead, buckthorn, cat’s claw, coral bean, golden creeper, green buttonwood, Jamaica caper, Jamaica dogwood, joewood, marlberry, mastic, myrsine, cassia, cocoplum, seagrape, Simson’s stopper, Spanish stopper, white stopper, snowberry, strangler fig, sweet acacia, wax myrtle, white indigo berry, wild coffee, and wild olive.
Habitat_Description: Matlacha Pass National Wildlife Refuge (564 acres) is managed by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service as a satellite refuge of J.N. "Ding" Darling National Wildlife Refuge. The refuge is located in central Lee County within the Matlacha Pass Aquatic Preserve. The refuge includes the original three small islands established as a preserve and breeding ground for native birds in 1908 plus 20 additional islands included in subsequent years, now encompassing 512 acres. The designation protects the lands from past and future development, including mining, fish camps and residential uses. The refuge islands are part of a highly productive estuary which supports a diverse array of wildlife. The islands contain two basic vegetative zones - upland sand ridges and mangroves. Several of the islands used as roosting and nesting sites for a variety of wading and water birds. The beaches and shores provide loafing, feeding, and nesting areas for migratory ducks, shorebirds, gulls, and terns. Ospreys, which are listed as a priority species in the Regional Resource Plan, can be observed nesting and feeding in Matlacha Pass area. Several endangered and threatened species benefit from the habitats described including bald eagles, wood storks, sea turtles, and manatees.

Project_Description: To compliment past hydrologic and oyster restoration projects, Sanibel Captiva Conservation Foundation undertook a mangrove restoration project in Clam Bayou. Red mangroves are the dominate species in the Bayou, but egress of red mangrove propagules for re-population is limited by the distance and connection to other seed sources. Red mangrove propagules were collected by volunteers from throughout the adjacent estuaries. Over 25 volunteers hand planted over 2,500 propagules along the shoreline of Clam Bayou. It is planned that the survival success of the propagules will be monitored in the future.
Habitat_Description: Clam Bayou (approximately 125 acres) is a shallow, mangrove-lined lagoon located on Sanibel Island between the Pine Island Sound estuary and the Gulf of Mexico, adjacent to the J.N. “Ding” Darling National Wildlife refuge. Water quality, temperature and salinity fluctuate widely due to variations in tidal exchange associated with storm events and pass closings due beach sand transport. . The primary habitats are mangrove wetland and submerged seagrass and mudflat habitats. Primary native vegetation species include red mangroves, white mangroves, black mangroves and shoal grass. The habitats support a wide variety of invertebrates, fish and mammals, including oysters, clams, killifish, mangrove snapper and many crab species. The surrounding land use is in residential and commercial use, with artificial waterways. The connecting pass between Clam Bayou and the Gulf of Mexico frequently opens and closes depending on storm and beach renourishment conditions. When the pass is closed temperature and salinity increase and water quality declines, causing fish kills algae blooms and hypersalinity in the bayou. The city of Sanibel, along with many partners, began a hydrologic restoration project in 2006 to add culverts to assure tidal exchange between the bayou, Pine Island Sound and the Gulf of Mexico. Oyster and mangrove restoration projects have been implemented by a number of parties in the subsequent years to compliment the hydrologic restoration.

The pine flatwoods and mixed pine/hardwood forests have high fire fuel loads and there are moderate areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Brazilian pepper, Australian pine, cogongrass, and old world climbing fern.

Project_Name: J. N. Ding Darling National Wildlife Refuge Hydrologic Restoration
Project_Description: This is a hydrologic restoration project at the 6,406 acre J.N. “Ding” Darling National Wildlife Refuge managed by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service. A large area of the refuge (2,619 acres) is designated as a Wilderness Area with limited access. Hydrology within the refuge is managed through a series of berms and culverts to assist with maintaining the diversity of wetland habitats for fish and wildlife use, provide public recreational opportunities and prevent flooding. FY13 hydrologic restoration activities included modifications to the double box culvert under J.N. “Ding” Darling drive to allow enhanced water exchange between wetlands and improve wetland, fish and bird habitat. The construction occurred before the beginning of the rainy season and restored natural hydrology to over 93 acres of freshwater and tidal marsh.
Habitat_Description: The J. N. “Ding” Darling National Wildlife Refuge (6,406 acres) is managed by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service. The refuge is located in western Lee County on Sanibel Island adjacent to Pine Island Sound Aquatic Preserve. One third of the refuge (2,619 acres) is designated as Wilderness Area. The refuge is a series of ridge and swales made up of several habitat types including estuarine habitat with open water, seagrass beds, mud flats and mangrove islands and interior freshwater habitats with open water ponds and spartina saltmarsh in the swales and West Indian hardwood hammocks on the ridges. Two brackish water impoundments totaling 800 acres are used extensively by wading birds and other water birds. The refuge has a large diversity of species. Several threatened and endangered species benefit from the habitats including eastern indigo snakes, American alligators, American crocodiles, wood storks, Florida manatees, Atlantic loggerhead sea turtles, Atlantic green sea turtles, hawksbill sea turtles, Kemp’s Ridley sea turtles, leatherback sea turtles, piping plovers, and smalltooth sawfish. Approximately 272 bird species have been identified utilizing refuge habitats, as well as 60 species of reptiles and amphibians, 33 species of mammals, and 102 species of fish.

Project_Name: Fritts Park and Preserve Native Vegetation Planting
Project_Description: The native planting component of the Fritts Park and Preserve habitat restoration is managed by the Calusa Land Trust. The site was previously in agricultural use and is being restored for habitat improvement and public access. The native plantings included 75 shrubs and trees including beauty berry, firebush, waxmyrtle, slash pine, cocoplum, lantana and others. The work was completed entirely by 25  Calusa Land Trust volunteers. The plants were purchased at a discount rate and delivered free of charge. The plants are watered routinely as needed and have a 100% survival rate 4 months after planting. The improved habitat will benefit the variety of bird and mammal species inhabiting and moving through the preserve.
Habitat_Description: The Fritts Park and Preserve is a 2.2 acre parcel owned by the Calusa Land Trust and Nature Preserve of Pine Island for preservation and restoration. The parcel is located in Lee County on north western Pine Island, adjacent to the mangrove wetlands that fringe Pine Island Sound. The habitat is disturbed forested wetlands, previously in agricultural wetlands currently being restored native vegetation with some mowed lawn for public use. Native vegetation includes live oaks, cabbage palms and saw palmetto. The parcel has very little exotic vegetation and no hydrologic alterations and supports a wide range of wetland invertebrate, bird and mammal species including bats, white ibis, eagle, piliated woodpeckers, bobcat and racoons.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Cape Haze Management Area Invasive Animal Control
Project_Description: This is a an habitat restoration project at the 20,343 acre Cape Haze Management Area of the Charlotte Harbor Preserve State Park managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. Restoration activities focus on prescribed fire and removal of non-native vegetation and animals, to improve wildlife habitat. FY13 habitat restoration activities completed included removal of 28 feral hogs, as well as invasive exotic vegetation removal, prescribed fire and road and trail maintenance.
Habitat_Description: The Cape Haze Management Area (20,343) of the Charlotte Harbor Preserve State Park is managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. The Cape Haze Management Area is located in the Cape Haze Peninsula between Charlotte Harbor and Gasparilla Sound in western Charlotte County. The tidal creeks include Catfish, Widden, Sisters Pond, Trout and Big Muddy, which drain to the estuaries and seagrasses of the Gasparilla Sound/Charlotte Harbor and Cape Haze Aquatic Preserve. The habitats include pine flatwoods, oak scrub, tropical hammock midden/mound, freshwater and salt marshes, mangrove islands and tidal creeks. The habitats support a great diversity of wildlife, birds, fish and native plants including panther, bald eagle, great blue heron, snook, sea trout and gumbo limbo. The pine flatwoods have high fire fuel loads and there are extensive areas of invasive exotic vegetation including melaleuca, cogon grass, guinea grass, Brazilian pepper and old world climbing fern. The Management Area is managed for habitat protection and restoration and public access.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Cedar Point Environmental Park Invasive Vegetation Control
Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 115 acre Cedar Point Environmental Park managed by the Charlotte Harbor Environmental Center and Charlotte County. Restoration activities focus on removal of invasive exotic plants to improve species diversity and wildlife habitat. FY13 restoration activities completed by staff and volunteers included treatment of over 100 acres invasive exotic vegetation, primarily Brazilian, as well as rosary pea, by hand cutting, pulling and treatment.
Habitat_Description: Cedar Point Environmental Park (115 acres) is managed through the Charlotte Harbor Environmental Center. It is located in western Charlotte County adjacent to the Lemon Bay Aquatic Preserve estuary. It is one of the last remaining large tracts of undeveloped land on Lemon Bay. The primary natural habitats include pine flatwoods, scrub, scrubby flatwoods, mangrove swamps, salt marshes, and wetlands, as well as submerged seagrasses in the adjacent estuary. Native vegetation includes sand live oak, myrtle oak, rusty lyonia, pawpaw, gopher apple, slash pine, saw palmetto, mangroves and marsh grasses. These habitats support a great diversity of invertebrates, fish, birds and mammals including bobcat, grey fox, yellow rat snake, gopher tortoise, pileated woodpecker, bald eagle, anhinga, black-crowned night heron and the great blue heron. There are some areas of invasive exotic vegetation throughout the park, including Brazilian pepper, rosary pea and Lygodium. The park is managed for habitat protection and restoration and public access and recreation. Trails and boardwalks provide bird and wildlife viewing.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Myakka River State Park Invasive Animal Control
Project_Description: This is an extensive habitat restoration project at the 37,199 acre Myakka River State Park managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. Restoration activities focus on prescribed fire and removal of non-native vegetation and animals, to improve wildlife habitat. FY13 habitat restoration activities completed included removing 1,111 ferral hogs and 1 African spurred tortoise, as well as prescribed burns and trail maintenance.
Habitat_Description: Myakka River State Park (37,199 acres) is managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection and is located along the Myakka River, a designated Wild and Scenic River, in Manatee and Sarasota Counties. A mosaic of 11 natural upland and wetland habitats occur in the park, including dry prairie, mesic flatwoods, prairie hammocks, scrubby flatwoods, basin swam, baygall, depression marsh, cypress dome, floodplain marsh, blackwater stream and 2 riverine floodplain lakes. The habitats support a great diversity of wildlife, birds, fish and native plants including bob cat, snapping and mud turtles, wood stork, sandhill crane, roseate spoonbill, cypress, oak and wildflowers. The pine flatwoods have heavy fire fuel loads and there are high numbers of feral hogs, and extensive areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Brazilian pepper, Melaleuca, cogongrass, world climbing fern, air potato, and hydrilla.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Gasparilla Sound is part of the Gasparilla Sound/Charlotte Harbor Aquatic Preserve and is managed to protect and restore submerged habitats, including seagrass, fish and shellfish. Bay scallop populations declined in the 1960s, primarily due to over harvest. Recovery of bay scallop populations requires adequate sources of larvae, especially following red tide events. Over 3 million bay scallop larvae, collected from nearshore waters in the Florida Panhandle, were released into Gasparilla Sound over healthy seagrass beds just prior to the stage in their life cycle where they settle onto the seagrass and develop into juvenile scallops. The purpose of the larval release was to provide adequate numbers of juvenile scallops to grow to adulthood and spawn the following fall in Gasparilla Sound. Monitoring of adult populations and next year’s recruitment of larvae is planned. The project involved local, state and regional agencies, as well as volunteers.
Habitat_Description: Gasparilla Sound (approximately 11,000 acres) is located in Lee County between the Cape Haze Peninsula and Gasparilla Island. Gasparilla Sound is connected to the Gulf of Mexico through Gasparilla Pass to the north and Boca Grande Pass to the south. It is part of the Gasparilla Sound/Charlotte Harbor Aquatic Preserve. It is a shallow healthy estuary surrounded by mangrove shoreline with little development and supports over 7,000 acres of seagrasses including turtle grass, shoal grass and manatee grass. The submerged habitats support a great diversity of fish, shellfish, invertebrates and marine mammals including oyster, clams, shrimp, mangrove snapper, snook, dolphins and manatees. Historically, bay scallops were abundant in Gasparilla Sound, but populations declined dramatically after the 1960s due primarily to over harvesting. Seagrass and water quality conditions are adequate to support bay scallop populations, but sources of larvae are limited and red tide adversely impacts fledgling populations.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Yucca Pens Wildlife Management Unit ATV Trail Ditch Blocks
Project_Description: This is a hydrologic restoration project at the 14,577 acre Yucca Pens Wildlife Management Unit of the Babcock/Webb Wildlife Management Areas managed by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission. Hydrologic restoration activities completed included blocking 23 ATV trail ditches with rock and installing 1 24” riser in the southeastern, as well as additional fencing and posting, in the southeastern portion of the Yucca Pens Wildlife Management Unit. The ditch blocks restored natural hydrology to over 1,000 acres of hydric and mesic pine flatwoods and tidal creeks.
Habitat_Description: The Yucca Pens Wildlife Management Unit (14,577 acres) of the Babcock/Webb Wildlife Management Area is managed by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission. The Yucca Pens Wildlife Management Unit is located in southwestern Charlotte County and northwestern Lee County within the Charlotte Harbor watershed. The habitats include primarily hydric and mesic pine flatwoods, with some freshwater marsh and oak scrub. The habitats support a great diversity of wildlife, birds, fish and native plants including Florida black bear, bob cat, coyote, otter, eagle, osprey, wild turkeys, great blue heron, mosquitofish and killifish, as well as invasive exotic feral hogs. There are moderate areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Brazilian pepper, Australian pine, Melaleuca, cogongrass, and old world climbing fern. Illegal ATV use throughout the Yucca Pens Wildlife Management Unit created extensive trails which act as artificial ditches and caused widespread hydrologic changes from natural sheet flow to channelized flow. The ATV trails are being reduced through fencing, posting and hydrologic restoration activities.
Main_Funding_Source: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
Lead_Implementer: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Siesta Waterway Pilot Mulching and Planting
Project_Description: Siesta Waterway Pilot Mulching and Planting project is one component of a larger goal to reduce erosion, provide greater habitat diversity and improve the natural aesthetics of the waterway. The Civic Association began 4 pilot projects to evaluate the effectiveness of different combinations of mulch and native plants at stabilizing the banks, reducing erosion, providing wildlife habitat and enhancing aesthetics, while successfully surviving the highly variable water level and flow conditions. The test plots (0.2 acres) compared sun vs. shade and hydro-seeding native seeds and mulch vs. native plantings within mulch vs. placing mulch around existing plants. In addition, in the existing grove of oaks, cabbage palms and palmettos (0.8 acres), the invasive exotic vegetation (including Brazilian pepper, Cesar weed and other disturbed weedy species) were removed, native species were planted (including beauty berry, fire bush, salt bush and stoppers) and mulch was placed around the plants. In addition to erosion control and habitat enhancement, the project reduces runoff and improves water quality flowing to Alligator Creek and the receiving Lemon Bay estuary. While the project restores only a small area of habitat, it provides large community stewardship and education opportunities, water quality improvements, research data on the effectiveness of restoration methods and partnership between the Civic Association and County for future components of naturalizing the waterway.
Habitat_Description: Siesta Waterway (5 acres) is located in western Sarasota County in a moderate density residential neighborhood in the City of Venice. Siesta Waterway was historically a natural tributary to Alligator Creek, joining the creek about 1 mile upstream from where it enters the upper Lemon Bay Aquatic Preserve estuary. The waterway was channelized as the residential area was developed and currently serves as part of Sarasota County’s stormwater management system. The waterway is approximately 7,000 feet long and the width varies from 10 feet at the bottom to 35 at the top. The waterway has freshwater, receiving much of its inflow from groundwater and water depth is about 1 foot, which varies by season and rainfall. There is slight erosion and a thick muck layer in the bottom of the waterway. The banks are relatively steep but not hardened with riprap and are covered with grass and some shrubby vegetation composed of mostly disturbance tolerant species. However, there is 1 grove of native slash pine, cabbage palms and oak species near the confluence of the waterway with Alligator Creek.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: J. N. Ding Darling National Wildlife Refuge Invasive Vegetation Control
Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 6,406 acre J.N. “Ding” Darling National Wildlife Refuge managed by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service. A large area of the refuge (2,619 acres) is designated as a Wilderness Area with limited access. Habitat restoration activities focus on prescribed fire, removal of invasive exotic and native vegetation and hydrologic restoration to restore the diversity of natural habitats throughout the refuge ridge and swale system. The habitat restoration projects improve wildlife habitat within refuge wetlands, as well as protect submerged seagrass habitats in the adjacent estuary. FY13 habitat restoration activities completed included 280 acres of invasive vegetation removal of Brazilian Pepper, Rosary Pea, Air potato and other species, as well as trail and road maintenance.
Habitat_Description: The J. N. “Ding” Darling National Wildlife Refuge (6,406 acres) is managed by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service. The refuge is located in western Lee County on Sanibel Island adjacent to Pine Island Sound Aquatic Preserve. One third of the refuge (2,619 acres) is designated as Wilderness Area. The refuge is a series of ridge and swales made up of several habitat types including estuarine habitat with open water, seagrass beds, mud flats and mangrove islands and interior freshwater habitats with open water ponds and spartina saltmarsh in the swales and West Indian hardwood hammocks on the ridges. Two brackish water impoundments totaling 800 acres are used extensively by wading birds and other water birds. The refuge has a large diversity of species. Several threatened and endangered species benefit from the habitats including eastern indigo snakes, American alligators, American crocodiles, wood storks, Florida manatees, Atlantic loggerhead sea turtles, Atlantic green sea turtles, hawksbill sea turtles, Kemp’s Ridley sea turtles, leatherback sea turtles, piping plovers, and smalltooth sawfish. Approximately 272 bird species have been identified utilizing refuge habitats, as well as 60 species of reptiles and amphibians, 33 species of mammals, and 102 species of fish.
Main_Funding_Source: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Description: Water quality improvement tasks included removing duckweed from the ponds and adding floating islands of vegetation to take up excess nutrients. Exotic vegetation was removed at a variety of locations throughout the preserve by volunteers during workdays. Hiking trails were cleared and a butterfly garden, bird watching area, education area with benches and kiosk were completed and an equipment storage shed was donated.
Habitat_Description: The Wildflower Preserve (80 acres) is a managed by the Lemon Bay Conservancy for habitat, fishery and hydrologic restoration, as well as guided nature walks. The parcel is a located in western Charlotte County between Lemon Creek, which drains directly into Lemon Bay Aquatic Preserve estuary and the Charlotte County Amberjack Slough Preserve. Wildflower Preserve is a former golf course comprised of saltwater and freshwater wetlands, submerged estuarine habitat and mostly disturbed uplands. Native vegetation includes a variety of mangroves, saltmarsh grass and seagrass species. Native upland species include oak species, cabbage palm, slash pines and a diverse variety of shrubs and wildflowers. The saltwater ponds on Wildflower Preserve are a rare nursery area for juvenile tarpon. Tarpon use of the ponds is currently being studied by university fisheries biologist to identify critical habitat needs.

Project_Name: Punta Gorda Management Unit Invasive Animal and Vegetation Control

FY13 habitat restoration activities completed included removal of 211 feral hogs and 70 acres of invasive exotic vegetation, including Brazilian pepper, shoebutton ardisia and cogon grass, as well as road and trail maintenance.
Habitat_Description: The Punta Gorda Management Area (5,572 acres) of the Charlotte Harbor Preserve State Park is managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. The Punta Gorda Management Area is located along the eastern shore of the Charlotte Harbor estuary south of the Peace Rivers in Charlotte County. The habitats include mesic pine flatwoods, scrubby flatwoods, salt flats, salt marshes, mangrove islands, tidal creeks and numerous embayments. The tidal creeks include Alligator and Silcox Creeks, which drain to the estuaries and seagrasses of the Gasparilla Sound/Charlotte Harbor Aquatic Preserve. The habitats support a great diversity of wildlife, birds, fish and native plants including bob cat, bald eagle, great blue heron, snook, sea trout and manatee. Project_Description: The Peterson 3 Acquisition is purchase of a 121 acre parcel comprised of 3 islands of undisturbed mangrove habitat on east central Pine Island, in the Matlacha Pass Aquatic Preserve estuary. The parcel was purchased by the non-profit Calusa Land Trust of Pine Island for preservation, restoration and public access to conservation lands. The parcel is bordered the on the north, south, east and west by the state managed aquatic preserve with submerged seagrasses. Acquisition of the parcel prevents the area from future development. The parcel is located on the Great Calusa Blueway paddling trail and visited regularly by canoers and kayakers. A management plan has not been developed for the parcel yet, but in the future Calusa Land Trust volunteers will conduct regular visits to the parcel to remove any invasive exotic vegetation or litter. Protection of the parcel and removal of any invasive exotic vegetation and litter will enhance fish and wildlife habitat in the mangroves and adjacent submerged seagrass habitats. Primary access to the parcel by volunteers and the public will be via canoe, kayak and shallow draft boat.
Habitat_Description: The Peterson 3 Acquisition is a 121 acre parcel purchased by the Calusa Land Trust and Nature Preserve of Pine Island for preservation and restoration. The parcel is located in Lee County, on east central Pine Island, in the Matlacha Pass Aquatic Preserve estuary. The parcel is composed of 3 islands. The primary habitat undisturbed native mangrove wetlands bordering submerged seagrasses in the adjacent estuary. The parcel has no hydrologic alteration and no apparent invasive exotic vegetation. The native mangroves support a wide diversity of mammals, including raccoons and bob cat, wading birds, including little blue and night herons, invertebrates including mud and mangrove tree crabs, and fisheries including mosquito fish, mangrove snapper and snook.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Highlands Hammock State Park Invasive Animal Control
Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 9,251 acre Highlands Hammock State Park managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. Habitat restoration activities focus on prescribed fire and removal of non-native vegetation and animals, to improve species diversity and wildlife habitat. FY13 habitat restoration activities completed included removing 214 feral hogs and 2 African spurred tortoise, as well as prescribed burns and trail maintenance.
Habitat_Description: Highlands Hammock State Park (9,251 acres) is managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection and is located in eastern Hardee and western Highlands Counties near the Highlands Ridge. A mosaic of 15 natural upland and wetland habitats occur in the park including mesic flatwoods, sand hill, scrub, scrubby flatwoods, depression marsh and cypress, as well as ruderal and developed lands. Native vegetation includes saw palmetto, slash pine, longleaf pine, cypress, several species of oak, hooded pitcher plant, gall berry, blueberries, and tarflower. There are several freshwater creeks including Tiger Creek and Haw Branch. The habitats support a great diversity of wildlife, birds and fish including scrub jay, swallow tail kite, snail kite, alligators, Florida black bear, Florida panther and bob cat. The pine flatwoods have heavy fire fuel loads and there are high numbers of feral hogs, and extensive areas of invasive exotic vegetation including soda apple, bamboo, Guinea grass, ginger lily, climbing fern, air potato and cogongrass. The park is managed for habitat protection and restoration, as well as public access and recreation, focusing on hiking.
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

An additional 10,000 juvenile bay scallops were raised to 5-20mm size, and 1,050 sub-adult scallops were released, also in seagrass beds. The project involved local, state and regional agencies, as well as volunteers.
Habitat_Description: The Aquatic Preserve native habitats include mangroves (red, white and black), seagrasses (turtle grass, shoal grass and manatee grass) and unvegetated submerged habitats which  support a great diversity of fish, shellfish, invertebrates and marine mammals including oyster, clams, shrimp, mangrove snapper, snook, dolphins and manatees. Seagrass and water quality conditions are adequate to support bay scallop populations, but sources of larvae are limited and red tide adversely impacts fledgling populations.
Lead_Implementer: Florida Sea Grant Extension Charlotte County
NEP_Name: Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership

Project_Name: Recovery Act: NE Florida Coastal Wetland Restoration Initiative FY11
Project_Description: Dragline ditches are extensive networks of deep, wide ditches and spoil piles cut through historical coastal wetland habitat, severely reducing the acreage of wetlands remaining. The purpose of the ditches was to interrupt the life cycle of saltmarsh mosquitoes by altering their breeding sites. A systematic process for restoring coastal wetlands that have been dragline ditched has been developed. Dragline ditch restoration projects require the use of an amphibious excavator. An excavator is mounted on tracked pontoons, enabling them to access submerged areas. This low-bearing weight machine (less than 2 pounds per square inch) is owned and operated by Volusia County Mosquito Control. Vegetation is cleared from the spoil area and placed in the adjacent ditch. This process avoids burning the plants and permanently sequesters the carbon they contain. Spoil material is first moved to the side of the ditch. If additional material remains, the main ditch is narrowed. The area of the spoil pile and the newly filled ditch are carefully graded to the adjacent remaining wetland elevation. The result is that substantially more area is at coastal wetland elevation. This technique was used to restore and reconnect impoundment T-18A to the Indian River Lagoon.
Habitat_Description: Impounded salt-marsh wetlands adjacent to the Indian River Lagoon.

Project_Name: POPPLETON CREEK TIDAL WETLANDS CREATION AND RESTORATION
Project_Description: Poppleton Creek Tidal Wetlands Creation and Restoration Project cleared exotics and removed upland areas in order to create tidal wetlands, then direct tidal flows into and through the overall property. The property’s configuration with respect to curves in the natural creek is advantageous to picking up the tidal flows at the east and west ends of the property and redirecting them through created mangrove wetlands and into the existing red mangrove wetlands from the south. It is a dynamic system, affected by both tidal influences from the South Fork St. Lucie River and IRL, as well as watershed inputs from a 667-acre urbanized area. Therefore, the City anticipated the results for the project to be dependent on these influences.
Habitat_Description: A forested wetland that has a small tidal creek and mangrove shorelines.  Clearing of exotics allowed upland portions to be modified to create more wetland area.
Restoration_Technique: Stream Flow Modification (including stream pool construction)
Main_Funding_Source: State of Florida Department of Environmental Protection ; City of Stuart Stormwater Utility Funds

However, pollution and overfishing caused significant losses of clams and seagrass across the Indian River Lagoon. At Haines, the site is sandy bottom with few grasses or hard clams. Project_Description: Coastal wetlands are among the most biologically productive natural ecosystems on Earth. Unfortunately, on Florida’s northeast and east-central coasts, wetlands were historically considered mosquito factories, uninviting wastelands with no inherent value. For decades, the Indian River Lagoon’s wetlands were filled, ditched and diked — mostly to control mosquito populations, with little regard for the other ecological values they provided. By the 1970s, more than 40,000 acres of coastal wetlands (approximately 75 percent of the lagoonwide total) were impounded and isolated from the lagoon. Pumping water into these isolated impoundments stopped most mosquito production, but also impacted the vegetation and many wetland functions. This project is phase 2 of wetland restoration, management, and water quality improvement to an impounded swamp adjacent to the Indian River Lagoon in St. Lucie County. Prior to impoundment, the swamp was a healthy mangrove marsh. During this phase the quad pump station was completed in the dike. The pump station helps to continue restoring this impoundment area to a more natural hydrology, allowing exchange of water to the lagoon. The quality, clarity, and circulation of waters of an additional 26-acre restored wetland and of the waters of the Lagoon immediately off shore from the project area are significantly improved by the restored filtering function of the mangrove marsh and seasonal pumping of waters into the wetland. Additional phases will add educational nature trails, and information kiosks to the site.

Project_Name: Restoration of dragline ditched coastal wetlands in Volusia County, Florida: Phase 1
Project_Description: Dragline ditches are extensive networks of deep, wide ditches and spoil piles cut through historical coastal wetland habitat, severely reducing the acreage of wetlands remaining. The purpose of the ditches was to interrupt the life cycle of saltmarsh mosquitoes by altering their breeding sites. A systematic process for restoring coastal wetlands that have been dragline ditched has been developed. Dragline ditch restoration projects such as this one require the use of an amphibious excavator. An excavator was mounted on tracked pontoons, enabling them to access submerged areas. This low-bearing weight machine (less than 2 pounds per square inch) is owned and operated by Volusia County Mosquito Control. Vegetation was cleared from the spoil area and placed in the adjacent ditch. This process avoided burning the plants and permanently sequesters the carbon they contain. Spoil material was first moved to the side of the ditch. If additional material remained, the main ditch was narrowed. The area of the spoil pile and the newly filled ditch were carefully graded to the adjacent remaining wetland elevation. The result is that substantially more area is at coastal wetland elevation.
Habitat_Description: Impounded salt-marsh wetlands adjacent to the Indian River Lagoon.

Project_Name: Indian River Lagoon Shoreline Restoration Project
Project_Description: This project restored mangrove habitat through community based education and hands on planting activities. This was addressed in two parts; the establishment, maintenance and monitoring of new and existing shoreline restoration sites was completed; and promotion of the project and awareness about the lagoon’s ecosystem through outreach and service learning was conducted. The program relies heavily on volunteer support with all aspects of the project, including assisting with monitoring, planting events, and maintenance at the Coastal Wetland Plant Nursery. The IRL SRP, currently managed by the FDEPand funded by the St. Johns Water Management District District and the Indian River Lagoon National Estuary Program, aims to re-establish fringing mangrove habitat along IRL shorelines while fostering community involvement and stewardship. Mangrove habitat along the shorelines of the Indian River Lagoon (IRL) has been in decline since the mid 1900’s. Mangroves are critical to the Indian River Lagoon ecosystem because they not only help to stabilize the shorelines, but they also serve as a nursery and safe haven for juvenile fish along with many other species native to the lagoon. The project was started in 1995 through the Environmental Learning Center (ELC), until 2008 when it was transferred to the Florida Department of Environmental Protection’s Office of Coastal and Aquatic Managed Areas (FDEP CAMA) Indian River Lagoon Aquatic Preserves Field Office. The project boundary extends from SR 528 in Brevard County to Jupiter Inlet in Palm Beach County.

Project_Description: 67-acres of borrow pits within the Loxahatchee watershed has been restored to natural wetland grades and planted with native vegetation. The 250-acre Jupiter Ranch tract is a portion of the cypress Creek basin in Palm Beach County, north of Indiantown Road and east of Gulfstream Road that was partially cleared and drained, primarily for agriculture purposes, most recently for cattle ranching. The western portion of Cypress Creek in Palm Beach County was most recently restored with funding assistance from the Loxahatchee River Preservation Initiative. The Jupiter Ranch Restoration Project, includes the removal of exotic vegetation from the project area, the restoration and creation of wetlands from areas that have been mined for shell rock, and replanting areas that have been cleared. The project began in spring 2010 with mechanical treatment of exotic vegetation. The mechanical treatment primarily focused on Australian pine from the spoil piles that were left behind from the shell mining and was followed by ground control treatment of exotic vegetation, primarily Brazilian pepper, Melaleuca, Australian pine, and Old World climbing fern in the project area. License Plate funding was used for the final phase of this project, restoring and/or creating approximately 67-acres of wetlands from the shell borrow pit areas. The areas were contoured to more natural wetland grades and elevations, then native vegetation was planted along trails, wetlands and buffer lands. A majority of the 67-acres of wetlands re-vegetated naturally.

A portion of the site is also located on the SE corner of Jupiter Farms Rd and Indiantown Rd. The natural area provides an important buffer for the Federally Designated Wild and Scenic Loxahatchee River. It also functions as a wildlife corridor connecting South Florida Water Management’s and Martin County’s Cypress Creek properties to the Loxahatchee River and Jonathan Dickinson State Park. Project_Description: Several attempts have been made to stabilize the shoreline of MC-2 by planting marsh grasses and mangroves on the island. Due to the intense wave energy in the area, the success of these restoration efforts has been limited. In an effort to implement a long-term solution to the MC-2 erosion problem, Martin County built a wave attenuation system to stabilize and protect the shoreline of MC-2. The wave attenuation system is essentially an off-shore breakwater comprised of limestone rock. The length of the system is 450 feet. The County chose this particular design because it provides the most effective means of reducing wave energy and has the fewest negative impacts of the available options.
Habitat_Description: MC-2 (Bird Island) is a ±2-acre dredged material deposit island in the Indian River Lagoon (IRL) located one-mile south of the Stuart Causeway, north of Saint Lucie Inlet and east of the Town of Sewell's Point. Bird Island is home to one of the most important bird-nesting colonies in South Florida including federally and state listed species such as wood storks, little blue herons, tri-colored herons, and brown pelicans. Coastal nesting sites are critical to the recovery of wading bird species like wood storks. Wading bird nesting in coastal locations usually occurs in mangrove areas similar to MC-2 that are surrounded by open water. Because of the island's close proximity to the intracoastal waterway, the eastern and northern shorelines of MC-2 are continually subject to erosion from boat wakes. Since 1970, the island has decreased in size by approximately 30% and recent hurricane activity has caused MC-2 to lose a significant portion of its plant cover.

Project_Description: This project employed successful subtidal, intertidal and shoreline strategies along 200 feet of shoreline of Indian RiverSide Park. The Indian RiverSide Park project is monitored pre parallel and then post-deployment once every 6 months for a minimum of 12 months. Martin County is tracking retention of mangroves, Spartina,  and oyster bags, growth of mangroves and Spartina, and recruitment of live oysters to oyster bags and concrete reef modules. Project education and outreach elements consist of interpretive signage at the project site, and dissemination of educational posters about the benefits of living shoreline restoration.

Project_Description: This project continues successful methods of living shoreline stabilization along an additional 80 meters of Turtle Mound shoreline. It includes deployment of: 1) approximately 600 mangrove seedlings (red + black mangroves) from locally collected seeds planted directly landward of the intertidal zone, 2) Spartina alterniflora transplanted from low-impacted regions within Canaveral National Seashore to create a meter wide band in the intertidal zone (approximately 400 individuals), and 3) placement of approximately eight-hundred 0.5 X 0.5 meter square oyster restoration mats seaward of the plants. One meter long shell bags are used for additional stabilization.Ongoing restoration has documented that this design satisfied this criteria as well as being an effective living shoreline buffer to further erosion. Turtle Mound Phase 2 deployment has been monitored after 1 week post-deployment then monthly for a minimum of 12 months. Monitoring will track retention of Spartina, mangroves, and mats as well as mangrove and Spartina growth and recruitment of live oysters to bags and mats. Shoreline stakes will be used to track erosion/accretion along the length of our restored area as well as control sites along the shoreline adjacent to Turtle Mound where restoration has not occurred.
Habitat_Description: Over the past sixty years, human impacts, including impounding, filling, and commercial and recreational activities have resulted in the destruction and alteration of many essential habitats throughout Mosquito Lagoon. Specifically, boat wakes from increased boating activities associated with the Lagoon’s national reputation for redfish and spotted sea trout have negatively impacted shoreline vegetation and intertidal oyster reefs. Areas where the vegetation and oysters are lost become bare, exposed shorelines prone to erosion. This has occurred at Turtle Mound, where once existed productive oyster reefs and salt marsh systems. These natural shorelines provided additional environmental services, including shoreline stabilization and protection, filtration of run-off from terrestrial sources, and served as habitat for numerous marine and terrestrial fauna, including many economically important fishes and invertebrates. Having oyster beds adjacent to salt marsh flora produced synergistic effects. Of particular importance, oyster beds protected salt marsh vegetation by buffering shorelines from wave action.
