Three acres of mangrove swamp and marsh have been reconnected with the creation of 300 linear feet of tidal creek that was newly built. Three acres of upland have been cleared. 14.9 acres of onsite coastal hammock area were cleared of non native invasive species and exotics including Australian Pine, lead trees, punk trees, Brazilian Pepper, and Malleluca, but two acres of coastal hammock vegetation, including acreage left unplanted from phase 1 were replanted or prepared for natural colonization by native species. Flow to approximately 2.25 acres of additional mangrove wetlands has been improved with the increase in depth, width, and length of three extant tidal creeks. Increased flow through Phase two activities resulted in the following improvements:  1,135 linear feet of three creeks includes the creation of a western tidal stream that is to become the connection for improved hydrology for the final phase. Over 900 hundred cubic yards of material have been moved or removed from the site including neglected construction refuse dumped on site before 1980.

Project_Description: One thousand twenty linear feet of Charles Ringling era (1920’s) seawall were in extremely poor condition on the eastern shoreline of Sarasota Bay. Located on the New College of Florida campus, the area is designated as a Caples-Ringling Estates National Historic District on the National Register of Historic Places. The failing gravity seawall was removed and a 1500 square foot dock was demolished. To maintain the integrity of the historic district, a new seawall was constructed along the southern 500’ of shoreline. The new seawall is topped by a historically correct balustrade and a wide esplanade. Along the northern 520 feet of the shoreline, a new intertidal lagoon was created landward of the historic seawall. The deepest part of the lagoon is -2 feet (NAVD 88). The lagoon has sloping intertidal shorelines planted in native bayfront vegetation. Several remnant sections of the historic wall serve as a temporary breakwater to protect the new lagoon.
Habitat_Description: Estuarine shoreline along Sarasota Bay, FL.

Project_Description: The goal of Tampa Bay Watch’s Community Oyster Reef Enhancement program is to increase oyster populations in Tampa Bay while improving water quality, reducing erosion, promoting fish and wildlife habitats, and increasing coastal resilience. The Lassing Park Living Shoreline Creation Project consists of the installation of two types of substrate (Lo-Pro Reef Ball™ units and oyster shell bags filled with fossilized shell) for oyster larvae to settle upon and grow, eventually forming a functioning reef:. Sporobolus alterniflorous was also planted. The oyster reef ball fields were constructed waterward of the oyster shell reefs and along mangroves to provide wave attenuation for erosion control and habitat for marine life.
Habitat_Description: The pertinent habitat located within the footprint of the Lassing Park Living Shoreline project consists of hard pack sand and soft sediment (silt/sand). Lassing park is a public use park.  As one of the few unarmored shorelines, this area is inundated with high energy from both wind driven and boat driven wave action.  Resulting in a substantial erosion issue at the northern end of the park.

Project_Description: The Philippe Park Living Shoreline Project focused on enhancing the shoreline at Philippe Park to reduce erosion and protect park property from sea level rise and storm surge; to improve water quality in Old Tampa Bay; to increase aquatic and shoreline habitat for oysters and other benthic organisms, fish, and wading birds; and to educate park visitors about living shorelines and coastal resiliency. Oyster bags were placed along two shoreline areas at Philippe Park (1,230 lf) from Oct 2021 through Apr 2022, and Spartina was planted as well. An oyster bar was created just offshore from Jul 2022 through Nov 2023 using oyster bags along a 720 lf perimeter and loose oyster shell within the area.
Habitat_Description: Oyster habitat in the form of shell bags and loose shell was built along the shoreline as well as offshore at Philippe Park. Spartina was planted along the shoreline as well.
Main_Funding_Source: County Capitol Improvement Funds, TBERF, County Pollution Recovery Funds

Project benefits include shoreline stabilization, improved habitat for birds and other wildlife, and improved water quality.

Project benefits include shoreline stabilization, improved habitat for birds and other wildlife, and improved water quality.
Habitat_Description: 1,043 acres of various coastal habitats including coastal upland, freshwater wetlands, and estuarine habitat on restored agricultural land and abandoned mining pits.

Project_Name: Boyd Hill Nursery Field Restoration Project
Project_Description: This long term restoration project hopes to transform an unmanaged uplands field to a native meadow. We are phasing the 8.5 acre restoration project out into manageable units. Previous units were prepped using herbicide applications. This current unit of .17 acres was solarized for 2+ months before planting. Nine varieties of native grasses were planted; a mix of plugs and one gallon pots. These initial units are giving us information on what plant varieties are most successful and what site prep techniques give us the best results. This info will determine the direction of the next plantings and restoration units.
Habitat_Description: Site was previously used as a municipal nursery, after decommission the area was returned to unmanaged field/meadow of approx. 8.5 acres. The site now has open access to hikers and park users as a trail system goes through it.
Main_Funding_Source: Boyd Hill Nature Preserve operating funds

Project_Description: Volunteers created oyster shell bags using mesh bags and clean oyster shell. Project benefits include erosion control, improved water quality, increase bird, fish, and shellfish habitats.

Project_Description: Chemical treatment for maintenance control of Brazilian pepper, lead tree, melaleuca, Australian pine and melaleuca throughout 2,300 acres on the southern side of the base.  Invasive grasses were treated through foliar application, and the tree species were primarily treated through basal bark application to kill the plants in place.  Following the initial herbicide applications, contractors were responsible to retreat invasive plant species within the project area until the plants were completely dead.  No further removal or treatment was required after the invasive species were killed, and plants were left to breakdown over time.  In addition, mechanical clearing of Brazilian pepper was accomplished on a 30 acre site which included an area of gopher tortoise habitat in the south central portion of the base.  MacDill also accomplished a formal survey of invasive species coverage throughout the 2,300 wooded acres being managed for control of invasive species.
Habitat_Description: Pine forest areas are largely historic planted pine which has not been managed for timber.  Areas of oak hammock and mangrove lined ditches are scattered throughout the pine areas and mangrove esturary predominates along the southern boundary of the site.  Additionally, there are large tracts of land within the site that have been historically disturbed (former landfill areas) which are highly invaded with Brazilian pepper.  Brazilian pepper, melaleuca, and lead tree are commonly found along the forest edges and scattered throughout the understory.  Open fields have scattered areas of cogan grass.

Project_Description: Mechanical removal of invasives and hydroblasting 10.8 acres of saltern restoration, 1.37 acres of estuarine highmarsh and coastal upland restoration. Project benefits include hydrology restoration, water quality improvements, increased habitat for birds, fish and shellfish.

Total Nitrogen reduction from the constructed cells averaged approximately 60%.

Project_Description: The primary project goal is removal of the upland mounds throughout the site to restore historic hydrology. The mounds are being removed using the hydroblasting technique. Exotic vegetation on the mounds is removed and the mound material is spread in 360-degree direction using high pressure water jet. Each mound is reduced to an elevation below mean high water to eliminate the uplands and improve tidal flow. Once the mounds are reduced below mean high tides, they will be planted with smooth cord grass. Phase II of the project is currently being permitted as additional funding is already secured
Habitat_Description: Extensive mangrove estuary that has been degraded through the construction of mosquito ditches, and creation of upland mounds.

Project_Description: The project dug up the mosquito ditch mounds, removing all of the vegetation including invasive species along a 1,200 foot length of historic mosquito ditch. A zone approximately 50 feet wide on both sides of the ditch was dug up to remove the mounds and vegetation. Most of the vegetation was chipped up, except for the largest oak trees and some palms which were set aside for re-use. Some of the fill was used to fill small sections of the mosquito ditch but the majority of the ditch as well as the mangroves along the ditch bank were not altered during restoration. The excess dirt was hauled off site and the disturbed areas of the site where the mosquito mounds were located (50 ft wide on each side of the ditch) were graded to a uniform elevation of +/- 2 feet amsl. This allows the entire site to be flooded during normal high tides. A 4:1 slope was created along the northern side of the site for the transition between wetlands and adjacent uplands. The large oak trees and palm trees removed earlier were placed back on the site (dead) to act as ‘structure’ or snags for additional habitat value. The western end of the mosquito ditch (outfall location of the ditch) was plugged to eliminate the potential for short-circuiting overland flow of freshwater (stormwater) during low tide conditions. Upon completion of site grading, the site was planted with 13,000 bare root marsh grass plants to help stabilize the sediment and create a marsh habitat. It is anticipated that mangrove (primarily Black) will recruit naturally across the site due to a large seed source in the surrounding areas.
Habitat_Description: Mangrove wetlands consisting primarily of Black Mangroves and to a lesser extent Red Mangroves along the edges of the mosquito ditch. The mosquito ditch mounds throughout the site were heavily invaded by Brazilian pepper. The site lies adjacent to a mixed pine and hardwood upland system.

In addition, 300 trees and shrubs were planted in a disturbed fill area formerly used as a dump site, 2,000 sea oats were planted along the north beach, and 18 maritime hammock tree species were planted youth camp site.

Project_Description: Habitats were undergoing succession. Hardwoods and vines were altering the composition of the habitats. As a result, quality gopher tortoise habitat was disappearing. Project_Name: Oyster Reef Shoreline Stabilization Phase IV
Project_Description: The project installed concrete oyster domes (reef balls) within the tidal flat zone approximately 50 feet seaward of the high tide line. Domes were placed base to base to create a solid substrate roughly 10 feet wide on which oysters could establish. The project constructed 1,890 linear feet of oyster reef using oyster domes (20,00 square feet in area) to protect approximately 1,600 linear feet of shoreline. Gaps were built into the reef to permit ingress/egress by marine life. The oyster reef helps reduce wave energy and trap sediment, eventually creating conditions suitable for establishment of salt marsh. A follow-on project will construct an additional 1,290 linear feet (4,300 square feet) of additional oyster habitat through the installation of 9,800 oyster shell bags. Eventually the site will be planted with marsh grass to further stabilize the eroding coastal system.

Project_Description: Work in 2013 included the chemical treatment of Brazilian pepper and other non-native, invasive species across two quadrants of the base (1,011 acres). Invasive trees and grasses were treated through a mixture of foliar application and girdling to kill the plants in place. Following the initial herbicide applications, contractors were responsible to retreat invasive plant species within the project area until the plants were completely dead. No further removal or treatment was required after the invasive species were killed, and plants were left to breakdown over time. The project area included 1,011) acres of upland forest and open fields (known as Quadrant 1, and Quadrant 2B). In addition, the mechanical clearing of live and dead Brazilian pepper was accomplished on a 10 acre site in Quadrant 3B.

Additionally, there are large tracts of land within the site that have been historically disturbed (former landfill areas) which are highly invaded with Brazilian pepper. Brazilian pepper, melaleuca, and lead tree are commonly found along the forest edges and scattered throughout the understory. Open fields have scattered areas of cogan grass.

Project_Name: Boyd Hill Nature PreserveøFreshwater Wetland Habitat Restoration
Project_Description: The project consists of construction of freshwater wetlands and coastal uplands within the Boyd Hill Nature Preserve in Pinellas County, Florida. Work includes excavation and embankment of two existing streams, re-contouring the stream bed and grading of side slopes to form ditch blocks and littoral shelves, installation and maintenance of existing culverts and stormwater conveyance structures, regrading an existing swale, and hydroblasting spoil berms into adjacent areas. The berms will require limited removal of exotic vegetation for access and clearing for planting areas. The creek bank will be planted with native species according to the planting plan. The measurable benefit is natural system creation/restoration of 30-acres.
Habitat_Description: The project consisted of modifying existing stormwater channels and back-filling ditches to restore natural flow and create wetland habitat and upland habitats within Boyd Hill Nature Preserve.

Project_Name: City of Treasure Island Living Shoreline
Project_Description: The living shoreline project was initiated to address ongoing issues with a failing seawall and erosion, habitat loss, and declining water quality along a vulnerable stretch of the Treasure Bay shoreline.  To protect and restore this coastal zone, a living shoreline approach was implemented using a combination of native marsh plantings and rip rap was strategically placed to reduce wave energy, trap sediments, and encourage natural vegetation growth. The intended outcomes of the project include stabilizing the shoreline, improving water quality, increasing biodiversity, and creating a self-sustaining, resilient habitat that can adapt to future environmental changes.
Habitat_Description: This living shoreline is a naturally stabilized coastal edge that mimics the structure and function of native shoreline ecosystems. It is characterized by a gentle, sloping transition between land and water, allowing for regular tidal flooding and dynamic sediment movement. The shoreline will be planted with salt-tolerant native vegetation, which help anchor the soil and provide vital habitat for fish, crabs, birds, and other wildlife.

Surveys done following prescribed burn conducted in June 2025 found 37 active gopher tortoise burrows on these former pinelands.  The goal is to continue to add native grasses and forbs to attain a more functional habitat for species present.  Over 12,000 individuals of native grasses, shrubs, trees and forbs were installed.

Project_Name: Newman Branch Canal Living Shoreline Tidal Creek Restoration Project
Project_Description: These canals have steep, unstable slopes that could be improved by transforming them into living shorelines.  Ecosphere offered to assist by securing grant funding from the TBEP to design and permit the implementation of a nature-based shoreline stabilization approach.  The resultant design also including creating a tidal creek system behind the former steep shoreline to increase estuarine habitat and provide a nursery ground for juvenile fisheries. Another successful P3 project!

Project_Name: Philippe Park Oyster Reef Wave Attenuation Barriers
Project_Description: Oyster habitat has been greatly reduced in Tampa Bay, and restoring this habitat, especially in Old Tampa Bay, is a goal for the area. Four reef dome wave attenuation barrier arrays were installed just offshore of Philippe Park to create wildlife habitat (mainly for oyster recruitment) and increase shoreline resiliency. A total of 76 precast concrete reef domes were placed to create approximately 2,432 sq ft of habitat. 32 of the domes were 3 ft tall by 4 ft diameter, and 44 of the domes were 3 ft tall by 5 ft diameter. A contractor placed 6 inches of crushed concrete base and then installed the domes to designed specs using a barge and heavy machinery.
Habitat_Description: Precast concrete oyster domes were installed to provide hard substrate for oyster recruitment and enhance wildlife habitat in an intertidal cove area just offshore of Philippe Park.
Main_Funding_Source: FDEP Resilient Florida grant, TBERF grant, Pinellas Co Capital Improvement funds

Project_Description: Three different elements were installed approximately 20 feet waterward of the existing seawall at Philippe Park to create oyster habitat and reduce erosion along the wall due to wave energy. Arrays of oyster castle blocks, an innovative concrete product from Virginia, were placed along 325 linear feet. 178 basalt mesh bags were filled with recycled oyster shell and placed along approximately 50 linear feet in a pyramid design with 4 bags on the bottom, then 3 bags, then 2 bags. Another 80 linear ft of plastic mesh oyster shell bags were installed as well. Oyster recruitment will be monitored.
Habitat_Description: Created approximately 450 linear feet of oyster habitat along southern-most end of Philippe Park seawall using precast concrete oyster castle blocks, basalt mesh oyster shell bags, and plastic mesh oyster shell bags.

Project_Description: When the Roosevelt Creek Ch 5 salinity weir was constructed in 1979, it interrupted the natural ebb and flow of nutrients between the watersheds and Old Tampa bay. This weir was identified as a prime candidate for modification to restore its marine connection, allowing for the passage of biota and a more natural hydrologic connection between the upstream channel and Tampa Bay. The removal of invasive/exotic species and the establishment of native plantings, as well as the improved conditions for mangrove recruitment are also major benefits of the project. This connection also has the potential for manatee incursion, thus a manatee gate was installed as well as one-way grates on all pipes connected to the channel.
Habitat_Description: Stormwater runoff from nearby urban areas flows into the channel and reaches the weir, where it widens into stagnant open water before spilling over into a brackish system. Upstream, stagnation and low oxygen caused frequent cyanobacteria blooms and fish kills. The weir was often overtopped by seasonal, unnatural/flashy saline backflow from Tampa Bay. Downstream, the channel turns brackish, with red and black mangroves and dense Brazilian pepper at the waterís edge.

Project_Description: We installed living shoreline breakwaters along 4 colonial waterbird nesting islands in Manatee County (Dot Dash Dit Critical Wildlife Area), and Pinellas County (Dogleg Key, Indian Rocks Beach Island, and Dunedin Sand Key West). The islands collectively host hundreds of pairs of nesting waterbirds from 15 species, including five state-threatened species and federally-threatened Wood Storks. To protect the islands from erosion and making them more resilient to sea level rise, we installed concrete reef ball breakwaters offshore to create a living shoreline. The linear arrays of reefballs are designed to be colonized by oysters, creating an artificial reef that provides wildlife and waterbird nesting habitat and improves water quality.
Habitat_Description: The islands are dredge spoil islands primarily vegetated with mangroves that have been experiencing erosion and toppling of mature mangroves due to vessel wakes, storms, and sea level rise.
Main_Funding_Source: National Fish and Wildlife Foundation Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund

Project_Name: Submerged Aquatic Vegetation (SAV) Planting at Lost River Preserve
Project_Description: Ecosphere was awarded funding to install SAV statewide to help expand the limits of SAV and this site was selected as a recipient site.  Two acres of native shoal grass and turtle grass were installed with in several locations with the estuarine basin to help diversify the habitat types within this restored site.  The shoal grass was harvested from this region and then hand installed by hand to inoculate this area with SAV.
Habitat_Description: This former habitat restoration site has been functioning well since it was implemented in 2009, however no SAV has naturally colonized the estuarine portion of this site, although the conditions were good for SAV.

Project_Name: Terra Ceia Preserve State Park Invasive Vegetation Control
Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 1,948 acre Terra Ceia Preserve State Park managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. There is an approved management plan for the park and management focuses on habitat protection and restoration, as well as public access and recreation.  FY24-25 Habitat restoration activities completed included treatment of 51.98 acres of invasive vegetation within 272.39 gross acres of park property, planting of native vegetation, and trail maintenance.

Main_Funding_Source: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission - Invasive Plant Management
Lead_Implementer: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission - Invasive Plant Management

Project_Description: This project focuses on selective herbicide application to Category 1 and 2 Florida Invasive Species Council's List of Invasive Plant Species within the conservation areas at Tom Bennett Park which includes areas of the park tidally connected to the Manatee River.
Habitat_Description: Manatee County's Natural Resources Department is tasked with managing Tom Bennett Park's conservation areas to reduce invasive and non-native plant cover.  The treatment of these invasive plants will support the native plant community and benefit wildlife.  Vegetation management is helping with the establishment of native trees planted in 2022 by reducing competition from non-native vegetation.

Project_Description: Roller-chopped 415 acres of mesic flatwoods and followed up with prescribed fire
Habitat_Description: Mesic flatwoods in the Upper Hillsborough Wildlife Management Area

Project_Description: The project entailed removal of the spoil mounds and all nuisance species. The mosquito ditches were either filled with the excavated spoil material to black mangrove elevations, dredged to promote effective diurnal flushing, or desilted to remove organics. Ditch blocks were installed at the end of ditches that were filled to prevent the movement of the placed fill material into the dredged or desilted ditches.  Nuisance species were removed from a few isolated spoil mounds with difficult access and planted with native upland species. Additional areas that exhibited saltern conditions were planted with appropriate species. This project will encourage the recruitment of mangroves, restore tidal flows, and improve fisheries habitat.
Habitat_Description: The restoration site at Weedon Island Preserve consisted of mosquito ditches and spoil mounds among a black mangrove habitat.  While the mosquito ditching created some red mangrove habitat, most ditches exhibited poor water quality from limited flushing.  The impounded ditches captured organics up to two feet deep which caused anoxic conditions. Very limited wildlife utilization was observed during initial site surveys including an absence of fish.
Main_Funding_Source: Pinellas County Penny for Pinellas Program
